bullets: The new EpiSEM-Bench release tests whether tool-using language-model agents act unsafely when a tool returns statements that are true but omits a safety-relevant fact. Its 300 matched safe and unsafe task pairs across six domains vary the missing evidence rather than the user’s benign request, separating evidence-recovery behavior from ordinary refusal behavior. Why it matters: If you evaluate agents that can take consequential actions, this adds a failure mode that standard harmful-request tests miss: proceeding because the environment supplied incomplete information. It can change whether a safety suite tests only what an agent was told or also whether the agent notices what it still needs to know. Evidence: E014. High confidence.

AgentPhishing is a new benchmark that evaluates whether adaptive, persuasive phishing messages can make language-model email agents both miss the attack and comply with its malicious request. It measures the agent’s response, not only whether it labels an email as phishing. Why it matters: If you are selecting an email agent that can access private information or act for users, detection accuracy alone does not establish safe behavior. This benchmark supports a separate deployment decision about whether the agent follows attacker instructions after its detector fails. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

The new NASICON retrieval-augmented generation benchmark packages a 52-question materials-science suite with results from 12 generators and multiple judge models. Retrieval-augmented generation means answering with information fetched from an external collection. The release also includes re-scoring runs, reasoning-ablation repeats, timestamps, software versions, and audit trails. Why it matters: If you are comparing retrieval systems or automated graders, this artifact lets you inspect whether rankings depend on the answer model, judge model, or evaluation procedure. That can change a suite-selection decision when a single automated judge would otherwise be treated as ground truth. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

The new MICA 2026 test release addresses training contamination in protein-model evaluation. It contains 30 cryogenic electron microscopy maps released in 2026, and every evaluated protein chain has no more than 25% sequence identity to any Protein Data Bank entry released before 2026. The creators also publish raw evaluation outputs and fixed-seed sampling details. Why it matters: If you evaluate systems that may have learned from historical protein structures, this split offers a clearer test of generalization to newly released and dissimilar proteins. It can change whether reported performance is interpreted as reconstruction of unfamiliar structures or possible recall of close training examples. Evidence: E012. High confidence.

AgentVQA is a new offline benchmark for vision-language models—models that answer questions about images or video—covering web agents, robotics, first-person video, games, and spatial planning. It is explicitly positioned as a scalable complement to costly simulator and real-world evaluations, not as their replacement. Why it matters: If you are choosing a suite for early agent-model screening, AgentVQA offers one common offline comparison across five interactive domains. Its stated role also clarifies the decision boundary: it can reduce the candidates sent to expensive live tests, but the supplied description does not establish that offline scores predict deployed performance. Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

The new specification-oracle-gap study audits coding-agent benchmarks for requirements present in grading tests but absent from the natural-language task description, such as exact constant names, module paths, or message text. It reports a static audit spanning five programming languages and distinguishes task completion from reproducing unstated implementation details. Why it matters: If you use test-graded coding benchmarks to select an agent, this changes how a failed task can be interpreted. Some failures may measure access to hidden project conventions rather than the ability described by the prompt, so benchmark maintainers can use the audit to identify tasks needing clearer specifications or separate reporting. Evidence: E028. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 EpiSEM-Bench 测试这样一种情况：当工具返回的陈述属实、但遗漏了与安全相关的事实时，使用工具的语言模型智能体是否会采取不安全的行动。它包含横跨六个领域的 300 组相互匹配的安全与不安全任务对，改变的是缺失的证据，而不是用户的良性请求，从而将证据补全行为与常规拒绝行为区分开来。Why it matters: 如果你评估的是能够采取影响重大的行动的智能体，这项基准增加了一种标准有害请求测试会遗漏的失效模式：因为环境提供的信息不完整而继续行动。它可能改变安全评测套件的测试范围，即究竟只测试智能体已获知的内容，还是也测试智能体能否意识到自己仍需了解哪些信息。Evidence: E014. High confidence.

AgentPhishing 是一项新基准，用于评估自适应且具有说服力的网络钓鱼消息是否能让语言模型邮件智能体既未能识别攻击，又遵从其中的恶意请求。它衡量的是智能体的响应，而不只是智能体是否将邮件标记为网络钓鱼。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择能够访问私人信息或代表用户采取行动的邮件智能体，仅有检测准确率并不能证明其行为安全。这项基准支持做出一项独立的部署决策：在检测器失效后，智能体是否会遵循攻击者的指令。Evidence: E002. High confidence.

新发布的 NASICON 检索增强生成基准提供了一套包含 52 个问题的材料科学评测，并附有来自 12 个生成模型和多个评判模型的结果。检索增强生成是指利用从外部集合中检索的信息来作答。该版本还包括重新评分运行、推理消融的重复实验、时间戳、软件版本和审计追踪记录。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较检索系统或自动评分器，这份评测产物可让你检查排名是否取决于回答模型、评判模型或评估流程。当单一自动评判模型原本会被视为真实标准时，这可能改变评测套件的选择决策。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

新发布的 MICA 2026 测试集旨在解决蛋白质模型评估中的训练数据污染问题。它包含 30 张于 2026 年发布的低温电子显微镜图谱，并且每条被评估的蛋白质链与 2026 年之前发布的任何 Protein Data Bank 条目之间的序列一致性均不超过 25%。创建者还发布了原始评估输出和固定随机种子的采样细节。Why it matters: 如果你评估的系统可能已从历史蛋白质结构中学习，这一数据划分能够更清晰地测试其对新发布且差异较大的蛋白质的泛化能力。它可能改变对报告性能的解读，即该性能究竟代表对陌生结构的重建，还是可能源于对相近训练样本的回忆。Evidence: E012. High confidence.

AgentVQA 是一项面向视觉语言模型的新离线基准——这类模型用于回答有关图像或视频的问题——覆盖网页智能体、机器人、第一人称视频、游戏和空间规划。它被明确定位为成本高昂的模拟器评估和真实世界评估的可扩展补充，而不是替代方案。Why it matters: 如果你正在为智能体模型的早期筛选选择评测套件，AgentVQA 可在五个交互领域中提供统一的离线比较。其明确表述的定位也划清了决策边界：它可以减少被送入昂贵在线测试的候选模型数量，但现有描述并未证明离线分数能够预测部署后的表现。Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

这项新发布的规范—预言机差距研究审计了编码智能体基准，检查评分测试中存在、但自然语言任务描述中缺失的要求，例如确切的常量名称、模块路径或消息文本。该研究报告了一项涵盖五种编程语言的静态审计，并将完成任务与复现未明确说明的实现细节区分开来。Why it matters: 如果你使用基于测试评分的编码基准来选择智能体，这会改变对任务失败的解读方式。部分失败可能衡量的是对隐藏项目惯例的掌握程度，而不是提示词所描述的能力，因此基准维护者可以利用这项审计识别需要更清晰规范或单独报告的任务。Evidence: E028. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.
evidence_items.title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. Phishing therefore poses privacy and security risks that depend not only on whether agents recognize malicious messages, but also on how they respond. Existing phishing datasets were developed primarily for conventional detection, leaving agent susceptibility to persuasive malicious requests insufficiently characterized. To expose vulnerabilities that pre-existing datasets may miss, we introduce AgentPhishing, a benchmark for evaluating whether persuasive phishing attacks can evade detection and induce LLM email agents to comply with malicious requests. We develop PhishOpt, which optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under fixed benchmark constraints and a realism constraint. We analyze the generated emails using Cialdini's persuasion principles to identify strategies associated with agent failures and use these findings to construct a universal generation skill. Our evaluation shows that agents can handle pre-existing phishing emails safely yet remain susceptible to attacks adapted to agent behavior, while in an AgentPhishing evaluation of nine agents, four exhibit phishing-detection rates below $10\%$ and malicious-request compliance rates above $45\%$. These results highlight the limits of inferring agent safety from conventional phishing evaluations and the need to assess how agents respond to persuasive malicious requests.
evidence_items.title: AgentPhishing: A Benchmark of LLM Email Agents Under Adaptive Attack

evidence_items.summary: Measuring animal distance and motion in metric units underpins abundance estimation, morphometrics, and movement ecology, yet monocular video lacks metric scale and wildlife datasets lack metric ground truth. We present WildDepth 2, extending the synchronized RGB-LiDAR WildDepth dataset in three directions. (i) Imaging radar: 37 RGB-LiDAR-4D-radar sequences (19,716 frames) with per-point Doppler velocity and a measured error budget, to our knowledge the first imaging-radar wildlife recordings. (ii) Benchmarking: a frozen, checksummed hidden test set for RGB-only distance estimation and RGB+sparse-LiDAR depth completion, evaluated separately on animal and background pixels. (iii) Motion and tracking: metric 3D trajectories obtained by lifting 2D tracks using LiDAR, radar, or monocular depth. Across 48,723 animal frames, object-level radar calibration improves monocular depth over scene-level LiDAR calibration without requiring LiDAR at inference (AbsRel 0.120 vs. 0.198), although animal-level LiDAR remains more accurate (0.052). Across 431 tracks, once-per-track radar scaling reduces 3D position error four-fold (2.20 to 0.58 m) and distance-sampling detection-function bias from -13% to -2%, matching once-per-track LiDAR calibration. Transferring radar Doppler onto LiDAR produces motion masks 3.7 times denser than radar alone at 72% precision, reduces moving-animal LiDAR accumulation error by 37%, and estimates radial speed (r = 0.60), albeit with approximately 50% underestimation.
evidence_items.title: WildDepth-v2: A Synchronized RGB--LiDAR--Radar Dataset and Benchmark for Metric Depth, Motion, and Tracking of Wildlife

evidence_items.summary: This dataset is the CryoAtlas v1.0 test set for research on automated protein atomic model building from cryo-EM density maps. The complete test set contains 16,657 curated entries derived from EMDB and PDB records available up to March 2026. Following map–model alignment, sequence mapping, and quality filtering, each entry provides paired experimental density maps, atomic structures, and protein sequences.This part is organized by complete EMD entries and includes density maps, corresponding atomic structures in CIF format, and original, aligned, and terminal-trimmed protein sequences in FASTA format. The four parts jointly constitute the fixed training split and contain no overlapping entries.This dataset belongs to the CryoAtlas v1.0 Package, which brings together all four training-set parts, the complete test set, and benchmark results. The package provides a unified access point for data retrieval, method development, and reproducible evaluation.

evidence_items.summary: Test dataset and raw evaluation output for a benchmark of MICA (Gyawali, Dhakal & Cheng, Communications Chemistry 2025) against EModelX(+AF), ModelAngelo, CryoAtom and EMProt for atomic protein model building from cryo-EM maps. The test set contains 30 single particle cryo-EM maps (1.95 to 3.92 Å) released in EMDB/PDB in 2026. Every protein chain of at least 30 residues has no more than 25% sequence identity to any PDB entry released before 2026, so none of the benchmarked methods can have been trained on these proteins or close homologs. Entries were deduplicated at 25% identity and sampled with a fixed seed (2026), 10 per size bin. evidence_items.summary: LongRS-Bench is a benchmark dataset designed to support long-term temporal understanding and reasoning in remote sensing vision-language models. It is constructed from multi-temporal satellite imagery and annotations derived from SpaceNet 7, SDSU MidWest Flood, and DynamicEarthNet, covering urban construction, flood evolution, and natural land-surface changes.The dataset contains 63,422 question–answer samples organized into four cognitive categories: evolution summarization, anomaly identification, spatial reasoning, and logical prediction. These categories comprise 12 subtasks that assess the understanding of temporal stages, evolution patterns, temporal inconsistencies, spatial changes, and future or missing states. Image sequences contain an average of 12.56 frames and a maximum of 28 frames. A subset of 5,000 samples provides structured reasoning annotations covering visual observation, feature identification, and evidence-based synthesis.The dataset is constructed through spatial and temporal preprocessing, task-specific question and answer generation, automated quality checks, and manual review. It supports supervised fine-tuning and systematic evaluation of remote sensing vision-language models, with an emphasis on integrating evidence across multiple observations to understand geographic evolution processes.
evidence_items.title: LongRS-Bench: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset for Long-Term Remote Sensing Cognition and Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.
evidence_items.title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence

evidence_items.summary: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding. The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure. A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions. The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion. Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.
evidence_items.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous research agents are increasingly used to automate large portions of scientific research, yet they are prone to research integrity violations (RIVs): behaviors that compromise the validity, reproducibility, or faithfulness of the research process. We present RIDAR, a framework for automated RIV detection and runtime intervention. First, we introduce RIVT, a comprehensive taxonomy of 14 RIV types spanning the full research lifecycle. Building on RIVT, we present RIDAR-post-hoc, a framework to detect RIVs within agent trajectories. RIDAR-post-hoc achieves 85.2% F1 performance on RIV-Gold, a benchmark for RIV detection with 60 expert-annotated trajectories. Applying RIDAR-post-hoc to RIV-Wild, a dataset of 300 agent trajectories across 50 distinct research tasks, we detect 3,964 RIV instances in 99.7% of trajectories, revealing the prevalence of RIVs in current agents. Finally, we present RIDAR-runtime, a framework for dynamically detecting and correcting RIVs during agent runtime. RIDAR-runtime effectively reduces agent RIVs remaining at task completion by 36.8%. We will release our code and data to facilitate future research.
evidence_items.title: RIDAR: Safeguarding Research Integrity in Autonomous Research Agents via Automated Detection and Runtime Intervention

evidence_items.summary: Bashkir is a low-resource agglutinative language written in Cyrillic and remains poorly represented in modern LLMs. We present an open resource suite and a systematic benchmark of adaptation methods: the Bashkir Web Corpus (71,567 documents, 46.9M tokens, 16 sources) and three labelled datasets for binary, multiclass and multilabel text classification; the benchmark covers the first two. Experiments use eight architectures (82M-8B: DistilGPT2, GPT-2 base/medium, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B, YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B, mBERT, XLM-R) and three adaptation groups (full fine-tuning, QLoRA, in-context learning), plus continual pretraining (CPT). (1) QLoRA on 3.8-8B models outperforms encoder-only fine-tuning on binary classification: YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B with CPT reaches macro-F1 0.748 vs 0.653 (XLM-R) and 0.650 (mBERT); pairwise differences are significant after Holm correction (p<0.001). (2) YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B significantly outperforms Mistral-7B and Phi-3-mini on multiclass classification, BPB and native-speaker ratings (mean 3.28 vs 2.52 and 2.22; n=100; alpha=0.69-0.77; p<0.05); on binary classification its QLoRA advantage is not significant (p>=0.084). (3) CPT effects depend on model and task: perplexity improves for Phi-3-mini (+0.58) and YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B (+0.33) but worsens for Mistral-7B (-1.15, p<0.001); on binary classification CPT helps Mistral-7B most (+4.0 macro-F1). (4) Tokeniser fertility on Bashkir varies 2.67x (2.92-7.80) and tracks adaptation quality, while perplexity across tokenisers is not comparable. Cyrillic tokenisers with Russian pretraining are preferable; LLM judges reproduce native ratings for grammar and coherence (rho=0.33-0.46) but not language correctness (rho=0.16, p=0.11); native evaluation remains necessary. All artefacts are open-licensed.
evidence_items.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models to a Low-Resource Agglutinative Language: A Corpus, Datasets, and a Reproducible Benchmark for the Bashkir Language

evidence_items.summary: Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite. These results suggest that partial-parameter CPT on a carefully curated corpus is a practical route to efficient MSA adaptation.
evidence_items.title: AQL-Lite: Enabling Efficient Knowledge Acquisition for Arabic LLMs via Data-Centric Continual Pretraining

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study aims to examine whether large language models (LLMs) can improve tourism demand forecasting accuracy compared to established statistical and machine learning approaches. Design/methodology/approach A systematic out-of-sample comparison is conducted using monthly tourism arrival data from Eurostat for eight European source markets. Benchmarks include optimized seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA), exponential smoothing (ETS), Prophet, Random Forest and seasonal naive models. Three LLM families are evaluated as zero-shot forecasters. Robustness is assessed across a pre-COVID stable period, a future period beyond LLM training cutoffs and an older model test. Findings LLM-based forecasts demonstrate consistent performance advantages over all benchmark models across countries and evaluation periods. In the main post-COVID period, LLMs achieve mean MASE values of 0.67–0.85 compared to 1.56 for ETS, 2.67 for SARIMA, 3.04 for Prophet and 4.32 for Random Forest. The LLM advantage persists in the pre-COVID stable period (LLM MASE 0.85–0.90 vs SARIMA 1.71 and ETS 1.31), indicating that the benefit extends beyond structural-break contexts. Robustness tests using an older LLM model and forecasts for a future period beyond LLM training data indicate that data contamination does not explain the observed performance patterns. Prompt ablation analysis reveals that providing contextual information (country identity and date labels) is the most beneficial design choice, while seasonal and shock hints offer no consistent improvement. Diebold–Mariano tests show directional evidence favoring LLMs in 31 of 32 pairwise comparisons, though limited test sample size (14–23 observations per country) precludes individual-country statistical significance at conventional levels. Research limitations/implications The analysis focuses on monthly national-level arrival data and zero-shot prompting.
evidence_items.title: Tourism demand forecasting in the artificial intelligence era using large language models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.
evidence_items.title: CellTrack-Bench: Microscopic Cell Tracking Benchmark for Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Offline tests can fail to reveal whether an agent update will remain safe after deployment. We operationalize this post-audit mirage using matched safe and harmful lifecycles that expose identical verifier-visible evidence while an isolated scorer records opposite deployment truth. Our theorem applies standard observational-equivalence and indistinguishability ideas to this executable audit boundary and states the resulting error-abstention tradeoff. The Post-Audit Mirage benchmark makes that boundary executable across authorization, scheduling, and shared-capacity environments. IdentifiedRangeMonitor uses fresh group-labelled harm outcomes to return deploy, hold, cannot determine, or unsupported. Experiments show that monitoring can recover the missing distinction in favorable settings but may remain undecided for rare groups, small effects, or missing observations. Verifier-agent evaluation must therefore test both calculation validity and whether the available evidence supports the deployment decision.
evidence_items.title: Post-Audit Mirage: Identifiability Limits of Offline Agent Verification

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.
evidence_items.title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence

evidence_items.summary: Ophthalmic clinical decision support requires fast, accurate, and privacy-preserving inference, yet autoregressive large language models (LLMs) incur substantial latency and computational overhead for decisions among predefined actions. We therefore investigate a decision-oriented alternative to generative reasoning. Specifically, we first introduce RetiJev-Data, a source-grounded ophthalmology corpus comprising 78,158 clinical-decision and diagnosis questions derived from articles in PubMed Central and a MeSH vocabulary covering 531 eye diseases, and 50,074 guideline-grading questions spanning 11 grading systems, along with a 24,662-question evaluation benchmark. Based on this, we develop RetiJev, a family of 0.8B-9B decision models that directly score candidate answers without autoregressive decoding. Across all model sizes, RetiJev outperforms both a 27B LLM and the commercial Jev 1.13 decision model on guideline grading by 10.4-23.0 points. RetiJev-9B further achieves the highest accuracy on clinical decisions, improving over both baselines by 5.4-6.5 points while matching them on diagnosis. It answers a case in 158 ms on one GPU, 3.5x faster than LLM generation and 470x faster than reasoning. Models are released at https://github.com/Awenbocc/RetiJev.
evidence_items.title: RetiJev: Fast and Source-Grounded Ophthalmic Decision Models

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise AI-agent evaluation needs evidence about whether test suites expose specified faults and whether their reference rules are trustworthy. We introduce REGATTA (Regulatory Evaluation of Agents via Two-stage Testing and Assurance), a measurement framework with three instruments. A 125-item source-cited checklist spans five industry-by-jurisdiction cells across the United States and Vietnam. A 25-fault corpus covers five categories, and a harness scores suite-level fault detection at the design and execution stages. We examine four measurement diagnostics on 180 generated suites (5,400 scenarios) from three LLM generators. A source audit finds 24 items misstating the rule in force, 46 additional citation defects, 31 items with only non-binding, unidentifiable, or unverifiable sources, and 24 verified clean. Only initially substance-flagged items received author review; all 24 clean rows received AI review only. Results therefore describe the instruments as written, not legal compliance. Item coverage varies, execution-stage fault profiles are stable across generators, and the historical stages agree on $66$--$69\%$ of fault--suite pairs. A current-model US-insurance retest finds stage disagreement above repeated-execution variation, but stage agreement $.536$ falls below pooled chance $.549$, failing V3's lower inequality. Blind adjudication by one expert supports the design-stage judging protocol ($\kappa=.72$, 95% interval $[.52,.88]$); 40 current-model execution probes give $\kappa=.75$. The instruments, audit, and reusable code are released.
evidence_items.title: REGATTA: A Cross-Domain Measurement Framework and Fault-Injection Harness for Enterprise AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have recently emerged as important remote sensing platforms, and UAV navigation has shown great potential in remote sensing applications. However, existing methods do not explicitly incorporate kinodynamic modeling or safety distances into trajectory generation, resulting in high absolute yaw rates, frequent collisions, and low navigation success rates, which limit safety and motion stability. To address this challenge, we introduce KinoUAV, a kinodynamic benchmark comprising a dataset and KinoUAV-Agent. First, we develop a hierarchical kinodynamic trajectory generation pipeline that drives UAV through acceleration actions. It uses waypoint chains from global planning and generates trajectories segment by segment under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints, reducing oscillations and improving trajectory stability. Furthermore, we introduce directional free-space distance (DFD) labels into the constructed dataset to describe the available clearance for safe motion decisions. The proposed KinoUAV-Agent predicts DFDs and uses them to generate safe actions, decoupling perception from action decision-making. This design enables autonomous obstacle avoidance and improves navigation safety. The benchmark incorporates the proposed Cruise-Seek task, in which the UAV first enters the target region and then searches for the target, reducing the difficulty of target search and improving navigation success. Experiments on KinoUAV show that KinoUAV-Agent outperforms existing methods, achieving the highest success rate while maintaining lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of kinodynamic modeling for safe and stable UAV navigation.
evidence_items.title: KinoUAV: A Benchmark for Safe and Stable UAV Vision-Language Navigation with Kinodynamic Modeling

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat. Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment. Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads. In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL). Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities. We constructed a comprehensive evaluation benchmark comprising eight textual and seven visual malicious categories, supplemented with benign datasets to rigorously test for false positives. Our evaluation across multiple leading LLMs, including Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash, demonstrates the efficacy and generalizability of this approach. The proposed method achieves up to 90.91% accuracy and 100% recall on textual tasks. In the visual domain, it achieves up to 99.28% accuracy while maintaining 100% precision across all evaluated models. Crucially, when evaluated against 500 highly obfuscated environmental web-agent injections (WebInject), MPIDetector achieved a detection rate up to 99.80%. Comparisons with two baseline approaches for detecting textual PI payloads, along with two additional methods for visual input detection, demonstrate MPIDetector's superior accuracy. These results show that LLM-driven reasoning provides a robust, cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injections.
evidence_items.title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection via LLM-based Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: The emergence of language-based AI agents promises to transform the scope of machine economic activity. Instead of just proposing bids or following hard-coded protocols, such agents can be used to negotiate and execute agreements in natural language. However, most evaluations of these abilities have focused on one-off exchanges or simple economic games, leaving open the rich space of time-extended, contingent, and incomplete contracts expressible in language; they also focus on raw profit, without measuring the qualities required for trustworthy contracting. We address this by formulating a rational framework for how agents should negotiate and perform natural language contracts in uncertain multi-step environments. Using this framework, we develop metrics and baselines for quantifying rational and cooperative play. We instantiate our framework in ContractSim, an evaluation suite where two players negotiate and execute a multi-turn supplier contract under environmental and inter-player uncertainty. We find that LLM-based agents agree on efficient contracts when environmental uncertainty is low, but under high uncertainty, often fail to negotiate satisfiable, efficient, or mutually beneficial contracts, underperforming even heuristic baselines. When executing contracts, LLM agents are also frequently uncooperative, violating contracts for extra profit even when they are easy to satisfy. These findings highlight room for improvement in the design of language agents that can negotiate and execute contracts both rationally and cooperatively.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Rational Contracting in Natural Language

evidence_items.summary: Automated Text-to-Speech (TTS) evaluation methods (Mean Opinion Score (MOS) predictors and Audio Large Language Model (Audio-LLM) judges) are expected to reflect human perception, yet it is unclear how well they capture the distinct aspects of speech that listeners actually perceive. We deconstruct "naturalness" into a linguistically grounded annotation schema spanning 10 distinct perceptual dimensions, and use it to construct the first dimension-level meta-evaluation benchmark for TTS, comprising 860 utterances annotated by trained linguist raters. Results from benchmarking four MOS predictors and four Audio-LLM judges reveal that MOS predictors are more sensitive to acoustic signal-level properties at the prosodic and paralinguistic levels, while Audio-LLM judges show selective, prompt-dependent detection that favors word-level errors and does not generalize across all dimensions. Neither class reliably captures a breadth of linguistically structured, human-perceptible speech errors. Our dataset, annotation schema, and evaluation code are publicly released to support more targeted and interpretable TTS evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Naturalness: Probing Automated Text-To-Speech Evaluators on Linguistically Grounded Dimensions

evidence_items.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks often describe a task in natural language but grade it with tests taken from the upstream project. Passing those tests can require information the description never states: a constant's name, a module path, an exact message. We call this a specification-oracle gap: where it exists, a benchmark also measures whether an agent reproduces upstream implementation details. We formalise the gap, including the inconsistencies that chains of dependent tasks add, and build a static audit for five languages that classifies every name-, path- and literal-level dependency of every scored test (held-out precision 89.2%, recall 92.9%). On SWE-Milestone (98 graded milestones, 35 published runs), 25 milestones contain a test that depends on an unstated, non-inferable name or path. Build units with such a dependency fail in 80.6% of runs, against 48.4% for comparable units without one, and withholding a single hidden name from the reference stops its unit's tests from compiling in 126 of 128 cases. The leaderboard's ranking is robust to removing the affected tests, but they shift scores within repositories and favour agents that reproduce upstream names. Across four further benchmarks, prevalence appears to follow construction: a third or more of the tasks are affected where specifications are release notes or LLM summaries, almost none where tasks are screened or written for their tests; how much a gap costs depends on how the harness grades. We release the audit, corrected filter lists and specification addenda.
evidence_items.title: What the Specification Did Not Say: Specification-Oracle Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Context: Multi-agent systems built on large language models now plan, call tools and execute code in production settings. Benchmarks measure what such agents can do, and separate efforts measure robustness to prompt injection, but no standard measures whether the orchestration platform that runs them is deployable: whether it terminates, behaves consistently, recovers from faults and enforces governance controls. Objective: We propose AgentGov-Bench, a benchmark that scores a deployed multi-agent platform on four separately reported axes (capability, reliability, governance and cost) and treats governance as eight behavioural invariants to be tested, not as features to be listed. Method: We define the invariants, a test procedure and pass criterion for each, a reliability protocol and a non-fungible deployability profile, and a reference architecture whose components map one-to-one to the invariants. As preliminary evidence we audited the official documentation of five widely used open-source frameworks against the invariants. Results: All five document bounded termination and human-in-the-loop approval as built-in features. None documents per-agent identity as a built-in feature; three offer it through an integration or hosted service. Built-in sandboxed code execution is documented by one framework. The documentation also records conditions under which controls fail open or do not cover all tool types. Conclusion: Feature availability does not establish enforcement. Deployability must be measured on the configured system with behavioural tests, which AgentGov-Bench specifies.
evidence_items.title: From Feature Lists to Enforced Invariants: AgentGov-Bench, a Deployability Benchmark for Multi-Agent LLM Orchestration Platforms

evidence_items.summary: LLMs are increasingly used as AI tutors, yet existing benchmarks overlook the challenging behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. We introduce TutorCaseBench, a benchmark that grounds AI-tutor evaluation in qualitative case studies from pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education. Our pipeline converts documented student categories into case-specific scenarios, tutor-student dialogues, and rubrics grounded in source evidence. The benchmark contains 923 dialogues across five challenge types, evaluated through open-ended response generation (1,560 items) and multiple-choice selection (2,537 items). Across 11 state-of-the-art LLMs, even the strongest model satisfies a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open-ended cases, while models are better at selecting appropriate strategies than generating situated responses. These results reveal a gap between intervention recognition and context-specific adaptation, especially for open-weight models. All data are publicly available at https://github.com/kixlab/TutorCaseBench.
evidence_items.title: TutorCaseBench: A Case-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Tutors in Supporting Students with Challenging Behaviors

evidence_items.summary: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce EvoForesight, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.
evidence_items.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.
evidence_items.title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic data generation (SDG) is the process of generating a new synthetic dataset based on the statistical properties of a confidential existing dataset. Differential privacy is the property of a SDG mechanism that establishes how protected individuals whose sensitive data is part of the confidential dataset are, when sharing such data. To ensure a SDG is differentially private, noise is injected into the statistics learned from the dataset. Depending on the amount of noise injected, we witness a trade-off between privacy and utility. Privacy is then measured via a set of privacy metrics that usually establish a lower bound on a few aspects of the privacy-utility tradeoff. Therefore, it is not possible to assess privacy based only on one metric. To close this gap, we demonstrate PrivEval, a tool to assist users in evaluating the privacy properties of a synthetic dataset. PrivEval implements several privacy metrics and validates them on both a single user and the overall dataset. Besides, PrivEval checks assumptions behind each metric. Hence, PrivEval is a first step to bridge the gap between privacy experts and the general public to make privacy estimation more transparent.
evidence_items.title: PrivEval: a tool for interactive evaluation of privacy metrics in synthetic data generation

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Short‐term temperature forecasts are useful in many IoT systems, but the models behind them are usually tested on one large public dataset rather than on the cheap sensors actually deployed. We ran one forecasting pipeline—a naive “no change” baseline and three machine‐learning models (Ridge regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) over lagged and rolling features—on two sources: the Jena Climate benchmark (Germany, 2009–2016, about 420 000 records) and 1 month of data from each of three low‐cost optical particle‐counter nodes in Tetovo, North Macedonia. All splits were chronological, and every evaluation was repeated with walk‐forward cross‐validation. Two of the three field nodes came close to the benchmark in absolute error (RMSE 0.76°C and 0.78°C, against 0.63°C on Jena) on roughly one hundredth of the training data, and two exported two‐feature models ran in real time on an Arduino MKR1000. The rest of the results were less comfortable. At one of those two nodes, no trained model beat the naive baseline, and walk‐forward evaluation showed the tree ensembles there to be far more unstable than the single split suggested. The third node's much larger error was not a modeling failure: its housing was heating in the sun, which we traced in the raw files and the site operators confirmed. Two further data‐quality defects, one per dataset, each changed a reported error figure. On this evidence, a benchmark score on its own says rather little about how a forecasting pipeline will behave on cheap edge hardware in the field.
evidence_items.title: Temperature Forecasting on Low‐Cost Sensor Nodes: What a Public Benchmark Does Not Tell You

evidence_items.summary: Abstract As modern systems evolve into complex microservices and highly regulated data ecosystems, manual test case design has become a severe bottleneck in Agile CI/CD pipelines. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) accelerates code synthesis, standard Generative AI models persistently struggle with the "Oracle Problem." They treat test generation as a stateless translation task, lacking the strategic reasoning necessary to navigate multi-layered industrial requirements without hallucinating logic. To bridge this massive "Design Gap," we propose the Agentic-QA Fusion Framework. This stateful, multi-stage architecture transforms automated test generation into an active reasoning ecosystem. Utilizing a specialized "actor-critic" loop comprising Parser, Triage, Architect, Writer, and Auditor agents, the framework autonomously strategizes, generates, and self-heals test scripts. The framework’s cross-industry scalability is empirically evaluated against baseline ML and deterministic LLMs across five complex datasets. This includes baseline commercial platforms (ISIS Travel, Travco Travel, Vantage Towers) and two highly constrained domains: the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) FIRDS system (requiring strict ISO 20022 messaging) and a governmental Job Matching Platform (JMP). By shifting the focus upstream to cognitive requirement analysis, the proposed framework successfully parses deeply nested regulatory logic. It drastically reduces hallucination and redundancy rates to 1.3% and 7.8%, respectively. Furthermore, it guarantees near-perfect syntactic correctness (99.6%) and achieves an industry-leading Mutation Score of 93.4%. Ultimately, while this Agentic approach necessitates higher computational resources to resolve dense enterprise dependencies, it establishes a reliable, zero-touch automation solution vital for modern software quality engineering.
evidence_items.title: AI-Driven Automation of Software Testing to Enhance Software Quality and Enable Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: Automated radiology report generation for multi-sequence brain MRI holds strong promise for alleviating radiologists' workload, yet it remains a demanding problem: brain MRI studies are inherently volumetric, each pulse sequence carries complementary diagnostic information, and annotated data are critically scarce for low-resource clinical languages. Existing brain MRI-report resources are still dominated by English reports, translated clinical text, or datasets adapted from task-specific imaging benchmarks, leaving routine low-resource clinical reporting and heterogeneous multi-sequence MRI protocols insufficiently represented. To bridge this gap, we introduce ViBMR, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale multi-sequence brain MRI dataset paired with routine Vietnamese clinical reports, comprising 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series across T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences. Building on ViBMR, we establish a comprehensive evaluation setup for brain MRI report generation, covering representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies. The results provide key insights into dataset characteristics and model behavior, while demonstrating the necessity of native low-resource clinical datasets for reliable Vietnamese-origin brain MRI report generation. Our dataset and baseline models will be released for non-commercial research.
evidence_items.title: ViBMR: A Large-Scale Multi-Sequence Brain MRI Dataset and Comprehensive Evaluation for Vietnamese Radiology Report Generation

evidence_items.summary: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.
evidence_items.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: When an off-the-shelf coding agent is used directly as a robot policy, observing a browser-based 3D interface through screenshots and acting by posing a virtual target gripper through a few tools, the agent's harness, its prompts, tools, and control rules, largely determines success, and until now it has been written by hand. We show that this harness can be improved automatically by another coding agent, the optimizer agent, and report two findings about what makes it work. First, the number of rollouts the optimizer agent sees per round governs whether the evolved harness generalizes: with rounds fixed, held-out success rises as the training batch grows from 5 to 100 rollouts, while small batches overfit the training tasks. Second, the optimizer agent must not be given free rein. Accepting every revision it proposes degrades the harness within a few rounds; a simple Champion-Challenger rule that promotes a revision only if it beats the incumbent on the same fixed cases turns the same loop into one that raises held-out success on LIBERO tasks from 51% to 67% over 30 rounds. The evolved harness is also a natural place to attach a pretrained policy, through one tool that hands it control. Distilling the rollouts of that combination back into the policy with multi-teacher on-policy distillation yields a standalone policy at 62.2% on RoboCasa365 under the official protocol, 4.8 points above its starting point with no harness at inference; the evolved harness on top of the distilled policy reaches 71.2% on the RoboCasa365 leaderboard benchmark, 13.1 points above the best published entry, and the loop closes when harness evolution resumes on the stronger policy. Automatic harness evolution for visual-interface robot agents is thus feasible, but its gains hinge on the rollout scale behind each decision and on how the optimizer agent's revisions are selected.
evidence_items.title: Scale and Selection: What Makes Automatic Harness Evolution Work for Visual-Interface Robot Agents

evidence_items.summary: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.
evidence_items.title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for Building Information Modeling (BIM) work, yet published evaluations test one or two models on a single task using simplified inputs, leaving practitioners without an evidence base for choosing between them. This paper’s contribution is a four-track benchmark of ten current models run inside one commercial Revit add-in suite on the production workloads of a working BIM department: requirement extraction from a live ISO 19650 BIM Execution Plan; rule extraction from an 88-page scanned Arabic building code; multimodal drawing review with live application programming interface (API) access, adjudicated and reconciled by two practitioners; and ten colloquial prompts executed in Revit, each carrying an adversarial probe. Scoring combines itemized rubrics, human verification, cross-model consensus and file forensics with telemetry from 218 logged calls. Three models form a leading group, Claude Opus 5 at 88.7 of 100, GPT 5.6 Sol at 86.2 and Claude Fable 5 at 84.7. Neither re-weighting the composite 20,000 times nor repeating the agentic track displaces that group or moves a composite by more than 1.8 points, but the separation inside it is smaller than that variation, so no ordering inside the group is claimed. On these prompts fuzzy name resolution, not code generation, accounts for 60 percent of agentic points lost, which argues for guardrails enforced in the tool layer rather than assumed from model behavior.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Production BIM Workflows Using Agentic Automation

evidence_items.summary: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.
evidence_items.title: Why Bother Me Again? Benchmarking Personal Agent Memory for Interaction Preferences

evidence_items.summary: DC-CoolTwin started as a workaround. We wanted to study how AI workloads, cooling water and cyberattacks affect each other in a data center, but there was no public dataset with all three on the same system. People usually use water-plant or industrial control data instead. We decided to simulate a data center ourselves. The dataset has four sites: Chittagong, Phoenix, Dublin and Singapore. Their climates are very different, which matters a lot for cooling water. Each site has 30 days of one-minute data (43,200 rows). Server load comes from real LLM traffic logs (BurstGPT, Azure 2024) and the weather is real too, from Open-Meteo. The simulator turns that into server heat, chiller and pump behavior, and cooling-tower water loss. We also attacked it. Seven attack types run for roughly 6% of the time: a fake temperature reading, a lowered set-point, replayed old data, a stuck water-level sensor, a drain valve forced open, and a network break-in that ends with tampered cooling settings. Besides 24 sensor columns and the attack labels, there's a column called water wasted L. It shows how much extra water each attack cost, compared with the same run without the attack. Water balance error is under 0.01%, and WUE stays between 1.77 and 2.55 L/kWh, close to real data centers. It should be useful for attack detection, adversarial testing, water forecasting, federated learning and cooling optimization. See README.txt for the columns.
evidence_items.title: DC-CoolTwin: A Physics-Based Digital-Twin Benchmark Dataset of AI Workload, Cooling-Water Consumption, and Cyber-Physical Attacks in Data-Center Cooling Systems
