evidence_items.summary: Institutions that deploy large language models in regulated settings often need technical evidence of responsible AI practices before approving a deployment. COMPL-AI provides a technical interpretation of the EU AI Act that organises this evidence under six principle groups and eighteen technical requirements, twelve of which current benchmarks can measure. The benchmark suites that produce this evidence are typically operated from a command line, while the staff who approve deployments are non-engineers. We present VERA, an open-source self-hosted dashboard deployed to facilitate responsible AI processes within a large European bank. A reviewer selects a model and runs public benchmarks against it. VERA scores the twelve requirements that current benchmarks can measure and instruments the energy consumed by each evaluation, adding run-level evidence for environmental impact. We run four served open-weight models through the requirement pipeline, and the dashboard displays a score for each measurable requirement. A within-subject study then compares how participants read these benchmark results: from the raw output files in one condition, and through the VERA dashboard in the other. The dashboard reduced the time needed to perform the responsible AI assessment, reducing the time required from 56 seconds using raw files to 30 seconds using our dashboard, on average. Our dashboard scored highly (4.36 out of 5) on usefulness in the survey conducted within the organization. The dashboard and the study material are released publicly to promote replicability and reproducibility in different organisational contexts.
evidence_items.title: VERA: A Responsible AI Dashboard for Assessing LLM Deployments in Light of the EU AI Act

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer-use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural-language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end-to-end benchmarks primarily emphasize long-horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub-element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH-Sheets), character-level grounding in long-text documents (POINTERBENCH-Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH-Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel-exact target geometry and evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI-Venus-2-9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH-Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine-grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.
evidence_items.title: PointerBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Fine-Grained GUI Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.
evidence_items.title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: As AI generated images are getting popular these days, discussions on such generations are widely existed in current public forums, software repositories, and photography tutorials. Moreover, with the help of LLM-assisted code translation, malicious actors can adopt such information to evade detectors without specialized knowledge or local GPU execution of the resulting tools. To evaluate such risks, we introduce \textsc{WildFakeToolBench}, a benchmark suite of $156$ executable image-processing tools derived from $220$ public sources across $142$ domains. Each tool retains its source evidence and passes syntax, execution, and output-distortion checks without using feedback from the evaluated detectors. On $105$ generated images from five generators, we evaluate six state-of-the-art detectors with images processed by the tools in our collected bench to assess their effectiveness against such in-the-wild risks. The strongest individual tools achieve attack success rates of $25.25\%$--$100\%$ across detectors, exceeding the strongest of six selected image-processing baselines for each detector. Evaluating subsets of an eight-tool pool yields worst-case coverage above $80\%$ for every detector. Effectiveness is sparse and detector-specific: high coverage across candidates does not imply reliable one-shot evasion. These findings not only highlight the potential of such web-sourced risks, but also show the potential on establishing AI-image detector robustness evaluation framework based on those in-the-wild information.
evidence_items.title: WildFakeToolBench: Benchmarking AI-Generated Image Detectors with Web-Sourced Image Processing

evidence_items.summary: Nepali-English code-switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code-switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two-stage synthetic-to-real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi-speaker, dual-engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross-domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (-1.88 pp) and switch-point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (-7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT-converged encoder-decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER-only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near-zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic-to-Real Code-Switched ASR: A Spontaneous Nepali-English Podcast Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.
evidence_items.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Domain generalization (DG) aims to improve the generalization of the model to any unseen domains. Targeting this goal, existing DG methods mainly focus on learning domain-invariant features or prompts from the given source domains. However, these methods rely on source-domain data, and collecting and annotating large-scale single- or multi-source datasets is often infeasible, limiting the practical applicability of DG. To tackle this challenge, we propose {\underline{Do}}main \underline{P}rompt Learning (DoP), a method built on a large vision-language model (e.g., CLIP) for zero-shot domain generalization, which recognizes unseen classes in unseen target domains without access to source-domain data. DoP essentially learns the target domain knowledge via prompt both in text and visual modalities to overcome the domain shift in text-visual modalities under the test-time adaptation formulation. Specifically, DoP first takes text domain learning (TDL) to simulate various distribution shifts by learning diverse style tokens implicitly in the text space with inter-style diversity loss and intra-style consistency loss. Subsequently, DoP employs visual domain learning (VDL) to further refine the target-domain-relevant style token generated by TDL by making use of the test visual data with self-supervised learning. Extensive experiments on popular DG benchmark datasets (e.g., PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet) and ImageNet show that our DoP consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art DG approaches. Codes are available at: https://github.com/shiming-chen/DoP.
evidence_items.title: Zero-Shot Domain Generalization via Domain Prompt Learning

evidence_items.summary: We present Protegrity-PII, a new PII decision model for structured and unstructured text. Protegrity-PII achieves a typed recall of 0.915 with a precision of 0.907 on a new benchmark we propose, PII-SCOPE. Our model processes text in 0.49 seconds per million characters at \$0.0005 per million characters on a single RTX 6000 using batched inference. Due in part to the expansive nature of the entity type taxonomy used in training, Protegrity-PII achieves superior out-of-distribution generalization when benchmarked against a selection of state of the art models and datasets.
evidence_items.title: Protegrity-PII Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, and they may not fully capture what the trace shows. We study this in a tool-use setting built on GSM8K, where agents call a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, giving clear ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported. We audit three trace-level detectors across six production models and 30 problems per model. Final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation can disagree in systematic ways. A key failure mode is silent tool-output override: the calculator returns a corrupted value, but the model later uses a different, often correct, value without calling the tool again, so the bad value stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review of 90 traces agrees perfectly with the automated labels for final correctness (67/67), fault impact (19/19), and fault relevance (18/18), but only 67/81 for verification; all 14 disagreements fall into four recurring patterns. Execution limits also change the reported result: in an ablation across two models, one ranges from 21/30 to 27/30 correct as step and token budgets change, while the other stays between 27/30 and 29/30. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should come with the trace evidence behind it, whether the question the detector asks applied to that trace, whether the run was cut off by an execution limit, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.
evidence_items.title: What the Trace Shows and What the Label Says: Auditing Behavioral Detectors in Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary:
Saliency and scanpath models are developed almost exclusively on natural photographs, yet paintings are composed by artists to guide the viewer's eye and differ from photographs in texture, colour and abstraction. We introduce \avatt, a free-viewing eye-tracking dataset on 
Images{} paintings spanning sixteen art movements and five centuries, with 
Scanpaths{} scanpaths and 
Fixations{} fixations from 
Participants{} participants (\spPerImageMin--\spPerImageMax{} observers per painting). For every painting we release individual scanpaths with fixation timing and eye--screen distance, fixation maps, saliency maps smoothed at one degree of visual angle, temporal saliency videos and rich art metadata. We benchmark classic and deep saliency models against human agreement, revealing substantial headroom for art-aware models, and rank 44 scanpath-similarity measures, including a new language-free family of image-encoder metrics built on ten CNN, ViT and self-supervised encoders. With controls that remove viewing biases, we show that faces are fixated  aceEnrich$	imes$ more than expected and within half a second, that local structure draws the eye, that composition rules fitted from image content predict where people look, and that art style shapes how much viewers agree. Dataset, code and a Python package are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Amine-CV/AVAtt.
evidence_items.title: AVAtt: A Free-Viewing Eye-Tracking Dataset and Benchmark for Visual Attention on Paintings

evidence_items.summary: Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover failures and manually encode new rules. We present SESAA, a framework in which an Large Language Model (LLM) agent starts from no rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable joern queries. The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic, which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean F1 of 0.742 across 8 independent runs, well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of 19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same repository. The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair.
evidence_items.title: Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling

evidence_items.summary: Unified audio models capable of audio understanding, audio generation and, increasingly, audio editing are proliferating rapidly. However, each capability is evaluated in isolation on specialized benchmarks and a basic question remains unanswered: can these models understand the audio they generate/edit i.e. do they exhibit audio understanding-generation self-coherence (UGC_OWN)? We introduce TORUS, an audio-native unified benchmark for holistic, closed-loop evaluation of unified audio models comprising 1,053 questions (117 tests) spanning 21 tasks and 8 audio domain settings across all 3 audio types. We evaluate unified models and cascades of specialized models across objective and subjective metrics. Best unified models are able to answer only 52.4% questions about their generations, while gpt-audio can answer 53.6% questions. We hypothesize that a truly unified audio intelligence should be highly self-coherent and thus position understanding-generation coherence as an essential test for future unified audio systems. Further details are on our project page: https://torus-benchmark.github.io/
evidence_items.title: TORUS: A Unified Closed-Loop Benchmark for Unified Audio Models

evidence_items.summary: Ensuring the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical for real-world deployment. However, current safety measures often fail to address implicit, domain-specific risks. To investigate this gap, we introduce a dataset of 3,000 annotated queries spanning education, finance, and management. Evaluations across 14 leading LLMs reveal a concerning vulnerability: an average jailbreak success rate of 57.8\%. In response, we propose MENTOR, a metacognition-driven self-evolution framework. MENTOR performs metacognitive self-assessment, using strategies such as perspective-taking and consequential reasoning to uncover latent model misalignments. MENTOR couples single-pass rule-guided inference for routine requests with a selectively invoked metacognitive evolution cycle that revises residual unsafe responses, distills successful corrections into a dynamic rule graph, and compiles validated rules into activation-level steering signals for future inference. Experiments demonstrate that MENTOR substantially reduces attack success rates across all tested domains and outperforms existing safety alignment methods. The code and dataset for MENTOR are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MENTOR-Evo.
evidence_items.title: MENTOR: A Metacognition-Driven Self-Evolution Framework for Uncovering and Mitigating Implicit Domain Risks in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.
evidence_items.title: VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)

evidence_items.summary: Motion instruction generation in cross-video comparison aims to produce corrective feedback that describes the differences between a query and a reference motion. However, existing models often generate instructions that exhibit motion hallucinations, failing to reflect actual kinematic differences between paired videos. To systematically investigate these hallucinations, we introduce MotionHalluc, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating motion hallucinations in paired-video comparison. MotionHalluc comprises 1540 fine-grained questions over 553 video pairs, evaluating hallucinations along three core dimensions: (1)directional hallucination, (2)attributional hallucination, and (3)temporal hallucination. Extensive evaluations of state-of-the-art large multimodal models demonstrate high susceptibility to these hallucinations. Furthermore, we provide Perceive-Parse-Verify (PPV) as a training-free measurements extraction and verification baseline that converts candidate instructions into executable measurement queries and supplies kinematic measurements at inference time. Our results show that this simple measurements injection yields an average 10.6% performance gain across models, suggesting that motion reasoning with explicit quantitative measurements is a key factor in reducing hallucinations in cross-video comparison. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Leocoding0971/MotionHalluc.
evidence_items.title: MotionHalluc: Diagnosing Kinematic Hallucinations in Fine-Grained Motion Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark scores often misrepresent a large language model's (LLM's) knowledge, because they rely, e.g., on the model's ability to follow specific formatting requirements. This especially penalizes base models that may know the correct answers but lack the ability -- typically introduced in post-training -- to structure them as instructed. To overcome this, we propose an efficient, automated, and architecture-agnostic method for model evaluation based on soft-prompt tuning. By optimizing only 10 soft-prompt vectors (~0.0006% parameters for a 7B model) over a short tuning period, we adapt models to specific benchmark formats, closing gaps in format-following and ensuring that underlying knowledge is accurately reflected in benchmark scores. We evaluate soft-prompt tuning across 7 models and 11 datasets. Our results show that (a) soft-prompt tuning saturates format-following within 150 steps (~1200 samples) while preserving knowledge accuracy, (b) it closely matches strong evaluation-harness baselines on well-studied benchmarks while requiring no manual benchmark-specific prompt or parser design, (c) it improves evaluation signal in settings where baselines are harder to transfer, including long-context datasets and instruction-tuned variants with different output styles, and (d) it produces cleaner outputs that improve agreement between exact match scoring and independent LLM judges. Overall, we propose a lightweight, automated, and flexible protocol based on limited-budget soft-prompt tuning for evaluating LLM knowledge.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Prompt and Parser Engineering: Soft-Prompt Tuning for Automated LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Computing a minimum $s$-$t$ cut in a graph is a solution to a wide range of computer vision problems and is often done using the Boykov-Kolmogorov (BK) algorithm. In this paper, we revisit the BK algorithm from both a theoretical and practical point of view. We improve the analysis of the time complexity of the BK algorithm to $O(mn|C|)$ and propose a new algorithm, the fast BK (fBK) algorithm, with a time complexity of $O(m|C|)$, where $m$, $n$, and $|C|$ are the number of edges, the number of vertices, and the capacity of the cut, respectively. We additionally propose a compact graph representation that allows our implementations of the BK and fBK algorithms to find a minimum $s$-$t$ cut in a graph with up to $10^9$ vertices and $10^{10}$ edges on a machine with 128 GB of memory. We denote these as $\texttt{cBK}$ and $\texttt{fcBK}$, respectively. Despite $\texttt{fcBK}$ having the better worst-case guarantee, we find $\texttt{cBK}$ to be the fastest available implementation within the family of BK algorithms when evaluating on a comprehensive set of benchmark datasets, highlighting the importance of memory-efficient implementations. We make our implementations publicly available for further research and implementation development within minimum $s$-$t$ cut algorithms.
evidence_items.title: Fast and Compact Graph Cuts for the Boykov-Kolmogorov Algorithm

evidence_items.summary: We present the first large-scale open-set benchmark for multilingual audio-video deepfake detection. Our dataset comprises nearly 350 hours of real and fake videos across eight languages, with 59% of data being generated. For each language, the fake videos are generated with several distinct audio and video deepfake generation models, selected based on their quality, via visual inspection. We organize the training, validation and test splits such that only a subset of the chosen generative models and languages are available during training, thus creating several challenging open-set evaluation setups. We perform experiments with various pre-trained and fine-tuned deepfake detectors proposed in recent literature. Our results show that state-of-the-art detectors are not currently able to maintain their performance levels when tested in our open-set scenarios. We publicly release our data and code for non-commercial use at https://github.com/CroitoruAlin/MAVOS-DD.
evidence_items.title: MAVOS-DD: Multilingual Audio-Video Open-Set Deepfake Detection Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: The dataset comprises 5,523 frames at 1920 × 1080 resolution (Full HD, 1080p), documenting forest floor environments in forested areas surrounding Warsaw, Poland. The dataset was collected using two smartphone devices: the Xiaomi Poco X5 and Apple iPhone 16. The images capture natural forest floor features, including fallen leaves, pine needles, moss, lichens, twigs, deadwood, exposed soil, small plants, and other organic materials. The collection represents the visual diversity of forest ground surfaces and vegetation under naturally occurring environmental and lighting conditions. Images were acquired using smartphone cameras, providing variations in color reproduction, sharpness, texture detail, and image characteristics between devices. All frames have a Full HD resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels, supporting detailed visual analysis and consistent image processing. The dataset is suitable for computer vision research, forest floor classification, ecological image analysis, vegetation and ground-cover identification, biodiversity-related studies, and the development and evaluation of machine learning and deep learning models. The files .0 are split regular ZIP archive for easier download. Please download all the files first. If you're on linux, please use zip -s 0 FILENAME OF DOWNLOADED FILE --out joint.zip; then unzip joint.zip. If you're on windows, please use Winrar, 7zip or similar app.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides 8,640 benchmark instances for the daily scheduling of a grid-connected battery energy storage system (energy arbitrage), based on the 5-minute regional reference prices of the five regions of the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM: NSW1, QLD1, SA1, TAS1, VIC1) published by the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO). From 1 October 2023 to 30 September 2026, the 5th, 12th, 19th and 26th of each month were selected, giving 720 daily price profiles of 288 intervals. Each profile is combined with three batteries (1 MW with 1, 2 or 4 hours of storage, 85 % round-trip efficiency, half full at the start and end of the day) and four model variants: A (LP, energy arbitrage), B (MILP, no simultaneous charging and discharging), C (LP with a degradation cost of 10 AUD/MWh discharged and at most one equivalent full cycle per day) and D (MILP version of C). All instances were solved with HiGHS 1.15.1 (one thread, cold start) on one computer: 8,619 are solved to proven optimality, and for the remaining 21 instances of variant B the best-known solution and a proven upper bound are given (largest relative gap 0.29 %). For every instance the dataset contains the profit, upper bound, gap, solve time and the full 5-minute schedule (charging, discharging, state of charge). Validation: a script (code/verify.py) recomputes every constraint and profit from the released files; LP bounds were recomputed from the solver's dual values; 180 instances were re-solved with an independent PuLP model and the CBC solver; every 5-minute price was checked against AEMO's trading price table, and the SHA-256 checksums of the 72 source files are recorded. Intervals with AEMO administered-price or market-suspension flags are listed in instances/price flags.csv.
evidence_items.title: A benchmark dataset of battery energy storage scheduling instances with verified optimal solutions, based on 5-minute prices of the Australian National Electricity Market, October 2023 to September 2026

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the experimental datasets, analysis-ready files, and reproducible R workflows generated during the development and characterization of an instant whey–pineapple beverage powder produced by spray drying. The dataset includes the physicochemical characterization of independent cheese-whey batches and Caqueteña pineapple (Ananas comosus (L.) Merr.) pulp, spray-drying processing conditions and responses, physicochemical and technological properties of the resulting powders, and panelist-level sensory acceptance data for the reconstituted beverages. Measured variables include pH, titratable acidity, density, fat or lipid content, protein, moisture content, ash, water activity, °Brix, color coordinates (L , a , and b ), powder yield, solubility, wettability, and hedonic scores for appearance, color, aroma, body, acidity, and characteristic pineapple flavor. The repository provides the original Excel workbooks together with CSV copies of the corresponding data tables to facilitate interoperability. It also includes R scripts for descriptive statistics, statistical comparison of whey batches, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of whey characterization, spray-drying responses, and sensory data, as well as generation of the sensory summaries, heatmap, and manuscript figures. An additional R runner script allows the main analytical workflows and graphical outputs to be reproduced sequentially. A README and detailed data dictionary document the files, worksheets, variables, units, wet- and dry-basis conventions, categorical codes, missing-value conventions, and replicate structure. Together, these resources provide a transparent and reproducible dataset for reuse in spray-drying research, dairy–fruit powder characterization, sensory analysis, and multivariate data analysis.
evidence_items.title: Dataset and R scripts for multivariate analysis, physicochemical characterization, spray-drying analysis and sensory evaluation of a whey-Caqueteña pineapple beverage powder

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the dataset and reproducible R workflow associated with a four-year field experiment evaluating complementary outputs of the Haney Soil Health Tool (HSHT) in two commercial apple orchards under organic and conventional management in northern Italy. Three organic amendments (digestate, green compost, and mushroom compost) were evaluated against orchard-specific controls in randomized complete block designs with four independent replicates per treatment. The two orchards represent distinct experimental contexts and were analyzed independently; they should not be treated as replicated levels of orchard management. The repository includes the plot-level dataset, a data dictionary, R scripts for data validation and processing, statistical analysis, and figure generation, machine-readable statistical outputs, final figures, and information on the R computational environment. The workflow independently recalculates and validates derived HSHT variables before reproducing the statistical analyses and figures associated with the manuscript. The research data, documentation, statistical outputs, and figures are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The R source code is released under the MIT License. Version 2.0 – October 2026 This version updates the R scripts and graphical outputs for Figures 2 and 3 to match the final manuscript. The changes include removal of internal figure titles and correction of the axis-unit formatting in Figure 2. A minor editorial inconsistency in the README has also been corrected. The experimental dataset, data-processing procedures, statistical analyses, and numerical results remain unchanged from Version 1.0.
evidence_items.title: Dataset and reproducible analysis for "Complementary Haney Soil Health Tool outputs reveal selective responses to organic amendments in apple orchard soils"

evidence_items.summary: A curated, quality-coded benchmark of experimental thermodynamic data for gas-brine systems: gas solubility, brine density, osmotic coefficients, vapor-pressure lowering, gas-phase water content, enthalpy of dissolution and brine permittivity, in single- and mixed-salt aqueous electrolyte solutions. 32,355 rows from 274 published sources in 11 families, covering seven benchmark gases (CO2, CH4, H2, N2, O2, C2H6, C3H8; 24 further gases are flagged) and six ions (Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Cl-, SO4 2-) over 233-773 K and 0.1-3,500 bar, including a CO2 + CH4 + water ternary family, and a separate supplementary tier of 7,803 measurements that the benchmark families cannot hold. evidence_items.summary: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports

A value of -1 means the node is discarded; any other value maps the node to a target node class. node types.json Node type definitions, each grouping a seed node with its positive and negative examples. evidence_items.summary: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.
evidence_items.title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents

evidence_items.summary: Public benchmarks drive research on vision-based safety monitoring, and the Safety Helmet Wearing Dataset (SHWD) has become the de facto standard for helmet-wearing detection. This paper reports a systematic near-duplicate audit of SHWD and measures how the contamination it uncovers affects the accuracy reported on the benchmark. A two-stage matching procedure—64-bit perceptual hashing with complementary thumbnail-correlation verification—shows that 2288 of 7581 images (30.2%) belong to 193 near-duplicate clusters, the largest containing 802 frames from one fixed camera, and that 421 of the 1517 official test images (27.8%; 22–29% across matching thresholds) have a near-duplicate counterpart in the training split, and a blind manual rating of 350 pairs finds that 100% of accepted pairs are frames of the same fixed camera (28% strict near-duplicates). Controlled experiments with YOLOv8n, three seeds each, quantify the consequence. With the test data fixed, removing the 1534 contaminating training images lowers mAP@0.5 on the contaminated test subset by 4.4 points, and a size-matched random control shows that the difference is not a data-volume effect; on the full official test set the inflation is 1.92 points relative to the deduplicated model and 1.35 points relative to the control. A cluster-disjoint experiment that holds the domain composition of the training set fixed shows that frames from the same cameras and sessions as the test frames add a further 0.6 points on those frames, so that most of the gap under the official split reflects the classroom imagery that the contaminating images supply rather than recognition of specific frames. Tracing images to their source shows that 97.1% of the test images imported from the SCUT-HEAD classroom-video dataset are contaminated, against 3.0–5.5% of the genuine helmet imagery, and that the effect is confined to the imported subset (+8.1 points there, −0.4 on helmet imagery).
evidence_items.title: Near-Duplicate Contamination in a Widely Used Safety Helmet Detection Benchmark: Audit, Controlled Experiments, and a Duplicate-Aware Evaluation Split

evidence_items.summary: The reliability of quadcopters is becoming increasingly important. However, the field of quadcopter fault diagnosis lacks a standardized, reproducible benchmark for fair and comprehensive algorithm evaluation. To address this gap, this paper presents RflyBench-FD, a standardized, open benchmark for quadcopter fault diagnosis built upon the RflyMAD dataset, publicly accessible at https://www.rflybench.com/competitions/5/ . RflyBench-FD establishes a complete evaluation framework that covers eight representative fault types and provides standardized simulation/real dual-domain splits, a well-defined task formulated as eight parallel classification sub-tasks, publicly released scoring scripts, and a multi-dimensional metric system (accuracy, F1-score, and robustness under Gaussian noise at 8/4/2 dB SNR and physically motivated sensor degradations) aggregated into a weighted composite score whose ranking stability is verified by a sensitivity analysis. To validate the benchmark, we evaluate twelve baselines spanning classical machine learning, temporal deep learning, domain adaptation, transfer learning, and training-mode ablations, complemented by noise tests, physically motivated sensor-degradation tests, leakage-oriented checks, and paired significance tests; the results show that the benchmark produces stable and discriminative rankings across method families. The platform further supports daily submissions, a governed real-time leaderboard with anti-overfitting safeguards, full result traceability, and an LLMassisted analysis report. By providing a fair, reproducible, and insight-rich evaluation infrastructure, RflyBench-FD aims to support the development and real-world deployment of robust fault diagnosis solutions for autonomous quadcopters.
evidence_items.title: RflyBench-FD: The Benchmark for Quadcopter Fault Diagnosis

evidence_items.summary: Agentic recommendation pursues shopper goals through sequences of context-dependent decisions. Developing and evaluating such policies requires faithful recommendation world models that capture both the interactive shopping environment and users' behavioral responses over long interactions. Existing resources rarely provide long-horizon, fine-grained real-user trajectories or support trajectory-level evaluation and offline validation against production A/B results. We introduce UserArena, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark containing 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users, spanning 566,102 items and 13 action types. UserArena pairs these trajectories with an interactive environment and supports offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test, enabling five-level evaluation from output validity and local decisions to sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes. To improve simulator fidelity over these long-horizon interactions, we further propose On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD), which uses trajectory-level intent to provide dense teacher targets on student-generated rollouts. Experiments show that OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity among the evaluated simulators under UserArena's evaluation protocol and most closely reproduces the production policy effect in offline simulation.
evidence_items.title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents

evidence_items.summary: Organic soils, including peatlands, contain large amounts of organic matter and can release greenhouse gases when drained or burned. This dataset maps organic soil extent and disturbance and estimates the associated emissions for 2001 to 2024 at 30 meter resolution. The maps and tables can help users examine where modeled emissions are concentrated and compare the contributions of drainage and fire. The downloads below include: A global map showing organic soil cover as a percentage of each 1 km cell. Separate maps of average annual drainage and fire emissions for each reporting period, also at 1 km resolution. Country and global summary tables, plus detailed results by country, climate, land use, drainage, and fire category. The maps are GeoTIFFs that can be opened in GIS software. Emissions maps report metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per cell per year. Summary tables are supplied as CSV files, and the detailed results are available in both CSV and Parquet formats. Results cover five reporting periods: 2001 to 2005, 2006 to 2010, 2011 to 2015, 2016 to 2020, and 2021 to 2024. Emissions are annual averages within each period. The final period spans four years. The model builds on the organic soil probability estimates developed by Isik and Hengl (2026) . We apply probability thresholds that vary by climate domain to define organic soil extent, then combine this map with land use, drainage indicators, and burned area data to estimate disturbance and emissions. The same probability layer and thresholds are used for all five periods. Emissions are calculated primarily using Tier 1 methods and default factors from the 2013 IPCC Wetlands Supplement. Please cite the Isik and Hengl source dataset separately when using the probability inputs. To request the 30 m model outputs as GeoTIFF tiles or a Zarr dataset, contact Erin Glen at the World Resources Institute's Land and Carbon Lab: erin.glen@wri.org .
evidence_items.title: Global organic soil disturbance and greenhouse gas emissions, 2001 to 2024: model outputs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Benchmarking has been the cornerstone of progress in computer vision, natural language processing, and the broader deep learning domain, driving algorithmic innovation through standardized datasets and reproducible evaluation protocols. The growing availability of large-scale Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) datasets has opened new opportunities for applying machine learning to aerodynamic and engineering design. Yet, despite this progress, large-scale standardized benchmarks remain limited for high-resolution three-dimensional automotive aerodynamics, making it difficult to evaluate and compare models systematically. In this work, we introduce CarBench, a large-scale standardized benchmark dedicated to high-resolution 3D automotive aerodynamics, and perform a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art models on DrivAerNet++, the largest public dataset for automotive aerodynamics, containing over 8,000 high-fidelity car simulations. We assess eleven representative model configurations spanning multiple modeling paradigms: classical neural operator methods (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), geometric deep learning approaches (PointNet, RegDGCNN, PointMAE, PointTransformer), transformer-based neural solvers (Transolver, Transolver++, AB-UPT), and implicit field networks leveraging triplane representations (TripNet). Beyond standard interpolation tasks, we perform cross-category experiments in which representative transformer-based solvers trained on a single car archetype are evaluated on unseen categories to probe generalization. Our analysis covers predictive accuracy, pressure-field fidelity relative to the CFD reference, computational efficiency, and statistical uncertainty in evaluation metrics, providing a unified comparison across modeling families and quantifying the robustness of performance estimates under shifts in test geometry distributions.
evidence_items.title: CarBench: A comprehensive benchmark for neural surrogates on high-fidelity 3D car aerodynamics

evidence_items.summary: Hydrogels are highly tunable soft materials, but their analysis is challenging because researchers have to coordinate dataset cleaning, schema interpretation, predictive modeling, conditional generation, evaluation, and reporting through independent task-specific scripts. Here, we present Agentic Hydrogel, a lightweight, human-in-the-loop (HITL) agentic framework for hydrogel data analysis and conditional recipe generation. The system combines planning, analysis, generation, and reporting modules while retaining human control over dataset selection, target assignment, and scientific interpretation. Deterministic modules perform preprocessing, model training, evaluation, postprocessing, and artifact generation, whereas an optional large language model (LLM) is restricted to summarization and does not control scientific decisions. The framework is demonstrated using a polyacrylamide (PAA) hydrogel rheology dataset and a granular hydrogel dataset where it successfully executes regression, classification, and conditional hydrogel recipe generation tasks. The results establish the ability of the framework to execute and produce documentation for machine learning (ML) workflows. Agentic Hydrogel is therefore presented as a reproducible workflow system rather than a new predictive algorithm or a replacement for experimental validation.
evidence_items.title: Agentic hydrogel: a human-in-the-loop computational workflow for hydrogel analysis and conditional candidate generation

evidence_items.summary: Data and code for "Climate change is decoupling fixed calendrical knowledge from the natural events it once predicted"   Jun Guo, Enze Song, Yi Liu, Lixiang Song, Xinyu Chang, Shengchu Zhang, Yang Xiao, Xinyi Liu, Yunhui Bai, Shuhui Yang, Xiaojiong Xu, Yongchuan Zhang, Hui Qin. Contact: Jun Guo (prof guojun@hust.edu.cn).   - Licences: dataset/ under CC BY 4.0 ; code/ under the MIT License (see dataset/LICENSE and   code/LICENSE , and section 4 for exceptions).   This folder holds everything needed to reproduce the results and figures of the paper. Many Chinese agricultural proverbs tie a natural event (river thaw, last frost, first snow, insect emergence) to a fixed calendar date such as a solar term, a nine-day winter period or a lunar date. We call that date the anchor . The anchor does not move with climate but the event does, so the number of days between them measures whether a proverb still holds. The paper evaluates 805 such proverbs at Chinese weather stations for 1951–2024 and projects them to 2100 with five downscaled CMIP6 models.   The folder has two sub-folders:   | Folder | Content | Size | |---|---|---| | dataset/ | Annotation layer of 20,606 proverbs, test units, station-year events, coupling results, projections, station and model inventories (14 data files + LICENSE ) | 21.5 MB | | code/ | Analysis and figure scripts, annotation protocol and validator, station list, map boundaries (19 files + LICENSE ) | 17.9 MB |     ---   ## 1. Conventions used in all files   - Dates are day of year (DOY, 1 = 1 January). Trends are Theil–Sen slopes in days per decade. - Offset = event DOY − anchor DOY, wrapped into (−182, 183] days so that a winter anchor paired with an   autumn event does not produce a spurious offset of about ±365 days.
evidence_items.title: Data and code for "Climate change is decoupling fixed calendrical knowledge from the natural events it once predicted"

evidence_items.summary: The development of modular artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires not only an architecture capable of coordinating specialized cognitive functions, but also a training-data strategy adapted to those functions. The composition, structure, provenance, and quality of training data influence the knowledge available to a model, the patterns it learns, and the capabilities it can develop. Treating the training corpus as a uniform collection of text therefore overlooks an important architectural question: what kinds of data are appropriate for different cognitive modules, and how should they be selected? This paper proposes a differentiated approach to training-data architecture for modular AGI. It considers two related challenges: the potential value of professional artifacts as structured material for specialized training, and the risks associated with sensitive technical content and the increasing presence of AI-generated material in publicly available text. Professional artifacts - including UX reports, product requirements documents, financial memoranda, technical specifications, incident analyses and the synopses that writers submit to publishers - already possess established structures shaped by professional practice. Their organization, terminology, and domain-specific content can provide a practical scaffold for segmenting and organizing training material. Rather than treating all source material as undifferentiated text, the proposed approach recommends considering professional documents as structured resources for developing specialized modules. At the same time, the information density that makes such artifacts useful may require particular care when they contain cybersecurity procedures, vulnerability descriptions, or other operationally sensitive information. A second challenge concerns the provenance and diversity of training data.
evidence_items.title: Training Data Architecture for Modular AGI: Corpus Quality, Specialization, and the Problem of Synthetic Contamination

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The complexity of preparing Merdeka Curriculum teaching modules and prompting constraints in generative artificial intelligence systems provided the background for designing the AIDERA (Artificial Intelligence for Digital Education and Research Advancement) website. This study aimed to evaluate the validity and practicality of the AIDERA application as an AI-assisted tool for preparing Merdeka Curriculum teaching modules relevant to educators' needs. Employing a Research and Development approach framed within the ADDIE model, this development evaluated a zero-prompt interaction mechanism based on parametric forms. Evaluation involved three domain experts and 23 teachers from SMK IPIEMS Surabaya. Data were collected using 1–5 Likert scale questionnaires supplemented with open-ended qualitative feedback fields to gather in-depth suggestions for improvement. Descriptive percentage analysis revealed an expert validation score of 96.67% (highly valid) and user practicality reaching 82.87% (highly practical). Document preparation time efficiency received the highest rating (87.83%), whereas operational independence and usability recorded the lowest achievement (79.13%). Qualitative findings highlighted several technical issues and system refinement notes, including the need for integrative tutorials, optimization of mathematical notation representation, improved responsiveness during simultaneous access, and content template flexibility. Although AIDERA demonstrates strong potential as a supporting tool for module preparation, objective evaluation regarding its impact on learning effectiveness still requires broader further testing. evidence_items.summary: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical research and publishing represents a transformative shift, offering unprecedented opportunities to streamline workflow efficiency, enhance language clarity, and accelerate scientific dissemination. However, this rapid technological adoption introduces ethical, epistemological, and procedural challenges, including concerns over data fabrication, automated bias, intellectual property infringement, and the erosion of scholarly accountability. A structured analysis of practical applications highlights a clear demarcation between acceptable supplementary uses and strictly prohibited practices. AI tools are unacceptable as co-authors, as authorship demands moral, legal, and scholarly accountability that non-human entities cannot possess. Similarly, generating or modifying clinical images and media using AI remains unacceptable due to the risk of data distortion and misrepresentation. Within the editorial domain, AI systems must not replace peer reviewers or editorial decision-makers. Uploading confidential manuscript content into external AI platforms violates author confidentiality, while automated algorithms lack the contextual judgment and critical reasoning necessary for peer evaluation and final publication decisions. Conversely, AI tools are acceptable for planning the structure of a manuscript, language and grammar corrections, translation, quantitative or qualitative data analysis, and formatting, provided their use is transparently disclosed and critically evaluated by human researchers. Ultimately, the ethical deployment of AI in medical literature hinges on the principle that technology must serve as an auxiliary tool rather than a replacement for human cognition. Human authors, peer reviewers, and journal editors retain full responsibility and accountability for the accuracy, integrity, and scientific validity of published work.
evidence_items.title: Medical publishing in the era of artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Peer review is important in maintaining the quality of scholarly publishing, but the process faces challenges such as shortage of reviewers, delays, inconsistent judgements, and overlooked errors. These challenges have increased the need to consider the appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in peer review. Completely excluding AI or allowing it to function as an autonomous reviewer may not adequately address these problems. A Human–AI Augmented Review model is therefore proposed, in which AI supports clearly defined tasks under human supervision, while reviewers and editors retain responsibility for interpretation, ethical judgement, and editorial decisions. Peer review involves both routine technical checks and complex scholarly evaluation. AI can assist with repetitive and rule-based tasks such as manuscript screening, consistency checking, reviewer identification, and identification of reporting gaps. Human reviewers are still needed to assess methodology, scholarly contribution, and ethical issues. Effective use of AI requires a clear division of responsibilities, verification points within the review process, and governance measures to address bias, hallucinations, confidentiality, and excessive reliance on automation. Careful and limited use of AI can improve efficiency and reduce avoidable errors while maintaining accountability and trust in peer review.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence as an Assistant in Research Evaluation and Peer Review: A Critical Case for Augmentation Without Replacement

evidence_items.summary: TheorySpace is a framework for distinguishing competing model families through sequential experiments. It tests whether one shared parameter within each family can explain observations across the measured experimental settings. Acquisition policies choose what to measure next; model exclusion requires a completed, sound infeasibility check. Families with unfinished checks remain retained. This software and data archive accompanies the research paper "TheorySpace: Joint Prediction Geometry and Checked Exclusion for Active Model Discrimination" by Myungin Lee. The main reproduction target is Study 4R: 368 designed synthetic worlds, nine acquisition policies, two repetitions per world and policy, 6,624 trajectories and 26,496 saved checkpoints. The archive contains the benchmark generator, policies, saved observations and outcome streams, independent rational checker, scoring and aggregation, historical descriptive resampling, focused checker-interface tests, and rigorous saved-checkpoint interval-enclosure verification. Earlier Studies 1–4 are outside the reproduction scope. After extracting the ZIP, run "python reproduce all.py" from the theoryspace-reproduction folder. The default saved-data workflow uses Python 3.13 and the standard library without network access. It reconstructs the reported results and writes machine-readable verification outputs. Optional commands support acquisition replay, supplementary sensitivity analyses and an external Bell-count numerical pilot. The README and accompanying method documents describe the commands, dependencies, expected results and limitations. The policy comparisons describe the evaluated benchmark and do not establish a universally superior acquisition policy. The external Bell-count pilot is a numerical integration example, not certified nonlocality or verified quantum realizability. The derived external count table is attributed to Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.4084706 and retains its CC BY 4.0 terms.
evidence_items.title: TheorySpace: Joint Prediction Geometry and Checked Exclusion for Active Model Discrimination (Code and Data)

evidence_items.summary:
AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact.
  Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners.
  AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input.
  It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame.
  We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses sim10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection.
  To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.
evidence_items.title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: LLM memory is widely used in long-term conversation understanding. Agentic memory systems often use mutation, structural organization, learned retrieval strategies, or other complex operations. Is this complexity always necessary? We study Raw-RAG, a naive RAG baseline using dense retrieval and reranking over raw history to supply evidence to a reader LLM. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME, and MemoryAgentBench, Raw-RAG ranks first among the compared memory systems in six of seven benchmark-model settings, outperforming the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13-5.53 points. We investigate why raw-history retrieval remains competitive. Evidence analysis shows that its higher coverage of necessary evidence can offset lower utilization. Useful evidence includes both answer values and the relations and dependency paths needed to derive them. Even complete access to transformed memory stores leaves an accuracy gap relative to raw evidence, highlighting the importance of preserving raw information. These findings challenge the necessity of complex agentic memory for the evaluated conversation tasks and establish naive RAG as an essential baseline.
evidence_items.title: Is Complex Agentic Memory Always Needed? Naive RAG Is Stronger Than We Thought

evidence_items.summary: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. The program is optimized jointly with its training data, using adversarial generation of counterexamples that target where the program deviates from the policy. We evaluate SCOPE on a benchmark of real-world policy tasks against prompt optimization, task decomposition, and workflow generation methods, achieving the highest average accuracy across tasks and models. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models without further optimization. This allows them to be deployed in production on inexpensive models, where they reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models. Unlike these monolithic models, SCOPE produces substantially more stable predictions, and each verdict is interpretable through the predicate outputs that produced it. Additionally, we validate the key components of our method through an ablation study. SCOPE thus enables reliable, interpretable, and efficient policy enforcement at production scale.
evidence_items.title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs

evidence_items.summary: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
evidence_items.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video

evidence_items.summary: We study intermediate sample-size efficiency for censored regression tests when the signal and significance level both tend to zero. Independent treatment assignment permits finite-sample conditional sign calibration under arbitrary outcome dependence. For stationary ergodic latent fields with independent smooth site noise, bounded scores learned from the same pooled outcomes retain their first-order drift under empirical squared-error consistency, without an estimation-rate requirement. An observable censored rank procedure consequently admits an explicit leading cost on long-range dependent fields with nonsummable covariances. Smooth response scores admit a complementary result without independent site noise. For observational fields, separated blocks and paired variance calibration control the dependence approximation at the nominal testing level and yield sample-size costs under explicit absolute-regularity envelopes. An exactly centered censored contrast removes unknown marginal centering under stated exogeneity conditions. We also give a product-limit construction for independent random censoring, information-loss identities, and directional score-bank comparisons. Numerical studies distinguish procedure loss, score-learning loss, and spatial variance inflation. A stationary nonergodic counterexample and an uncensored Gaussian benchmark delimit the field results. Independent-data proofs, finite-range constructions, and a finite-dimensional measurement extension are included in the same manuscript.
evidence_items.title: Intermediate efficiency of censored regression tests on stationary random fields

evidence_items.summary: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.
evidence_items.title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters

evidence_items.summary: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard for building information exchange in architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC), is increasingly queried through large language models (LLMs) using natural language. Evaluating these systems at scale is difficult because free-text answers require costly human or LLM-based review. We propose IFC-MCQ, a method that automatically generates multiple-choice benchmarks from IFC files for exact option-set grading. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes across four groups, with answer keys derived from the file and distractors constructed from file-derived values or predefined rules. We applied IFC-MCQ to IFC models of varying sizes and modelling characteristics to assess generation coverage and evaluated two agentic configurations on selected models using tool- and code-based retrieval. The evaluation exposed category-specific failure modes and showed that performance can vary with the source IFC model and retrieval interface. IFC-MCQ enables scalable benchmarking of LLM-based IFC retrieval in AEC workflows.

evidence_items.summary: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS's pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question-answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22%-33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4%-22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.
evidence_items.title: Synthesis of Reliable Logic Question Answering Data for Large Language Model with Aid of Operations Research Program

evidence_items.summary: Aim: Global Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with cultural nuances. This pilot study investigates the feasibility of “Kumru,” a developing native Turkish LLM, in interpreting culturally specific emergency triage vignettes compared to standard medical terminology.Materials and Methods: A prospective in-silico study was conducted using a pilot dataset of 50 clinical vignettes based on Turkish Ministry of Health (Annex-4) Guidelines. The dataset was stratified into standard medical terminology (n=31) and cultural idioms (n=19) to assess domain-specific linguistic processing.Results: The model achieved 93.7% sensitivity for high-acuity cases but exhibited a specificity of 0% and an over-triage rate of 52%. While overall diagnostic accuracy was moderate (44.0%), the model demonstrated statistically superior performance in decoding cultural idioms (84.2%) compared to standard terminology (19.3%, p &lt; .001).Conclusions: Although the current native model demonstrates a high capability for understanding local idioms, its low specificity renders it operationally inefficient for autonomous clinical decision-making. These findings present a proof-of-concept for linguistic localization but highlight the necessity for extensive fine-tuning before clinical deployment.
evidence_items.title: Preliminary evaluation of a native Turkish large language model in emergency triage: a pilot study on cultural vs. standard terminology

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background The increasing availability of machine-readable research data has created a growing need for efficient large-scale data harmonization (DH). Although large language models (LLMs) show promise for reducing the time and labor required for DH, their effective integration into harmonization workflows remains an important methodological challenge. Objective This study aims to develop and evaluate a semiautomated, human-in-the-loop (HITL) LLM-assisted DH workflow as a proof of concept across 8 projects within a research consortium focused on disparities in multiple chronic conditions. Methods We developed an LLM-assisted DH workflow that combined preprocessing, semantic mapping, variable response mapping, synthetic data generation, data transformation, and iterative researcher review. Using Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT-4o) hosted in a secure academic environment, project-specific survey items were mapped to 114 Consortium Common Data Element (CDE) semantic groups. Semantic mapping accuracy was evaluated based on the Consortium’s consensus harmonization results. Complete and incomplete semantic mappings were distinguished according to construct overlap, and incomplete mappings requiring context-dependent human judgment were excluded for mapped item pairs and CDE semantic groups with and without HITL review. Results Following preprocessing, 884 survey items were included in the DH workflow, of which 812 were mapped to a mean of 79 CDE semantic groups per project. Mean semantic mapping accuracy for item pairs was 95.9% (SD 5.7%) with HITL review and 86.7% (SD 8.6%) without HITL review. At the CDE semantic-group level, the corresponding accuracies were 98.9% (SD 1.7%) and 94.9% (SD 4.0%), respectively. Across projects, omission of valid semantic mappings occurred more frequently than incorrect semantic mappings, particularly for heterogeneous response structures and subjective constructs measured using different instruments.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Semiautomated Data Harmonization Pipeline for the Multiple Chronic Disease Disparities Research Consortium: Framework Development and Comparative Validation Study

evidence_items.summary: Although social media has become a central arena for deliberative discourse, debates are frequently characterized by incivility. Due to the volume of online discourse, it is challenging to assess when and where interventions, such as community-based counterspeech, are required. Accordingly, automated measurement of deliberative quality is a powerful tool for facilitating constructive online communication. Since deliberation is multidimensional, attempts to monitor online discourse must consider alternative forms of communication to foster inclusive deliberation. Whereas Type I deliberative dimensions, such as rationality and civility, are grounded in Habermasian ideals, Type II deliberation extends this perspective by incorporating alternative communicative forms, including emotionality and storytelling, into a more inclusive assessment of deliberative quality. Addressing the limitations of prior studies that primarily focused on classic Type I deliberative dimensions and tested only a small number of large language models, this study evaluates multiple open-weight models to conduct a nuanced assessment of deliberative quality. We applied the large language model that achieved the best overall balance between predictive performance, model size, and computational efficiency to a dataset of 64,223 comments from German-language climate change discourse on X. Our results demonstrate that large language models can reliably capture complex Type II deliberative dimensions despite class imbalances and subtle linguistic cues that generally hinder automated text classification. Class imbalance often impairs classification performance due to highly skewed label distributions, and Type II dimensions are particularly difficult to detect as they are often signaled by implicit, context-dependent markers.
evidence_items.title: Can AI Gauge Deliberative Quality? Evaluating Deliberation on Social Media With Large Language Models
