evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine learning has moved from proof of concept to routine operation in pharmaceutical quality control, yet the autonomy it is granted narrows sharply as products approach release. In this narrative review, we propose that this unevenness reflects not model capability but the regulatory burden an output must clear before it can be acted on, a pattern we term the validation‐barrier gradient. We score this barrier across four stages on criteria covering decision criticality under good manufacturing practice, validation and data‐integrity load, locus of legal liability, and patient‐safety consequence. The composite barrier rises as observed autonomy falls. At final product inspection, deep vision systems already detect defects at line speed, often on small single‐site datasets, but the authority to release a batch still rests with a qualified person. This gap between what a model can do and what it is allowed to decide cannot be explained by task difficulty alone. Closing it requires not further accuracy gains but shared benchmarks, routine robustness reporting, and change‐control pathways allowing validated models to be updated rather than frozen.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical drug product quality control and assurance

evidence_items.summary: The excess energy and pressure of a strongly screened Yukawa fluid (screening parameter κ in the range of 5 ≤ κ ≤ 12) are calculated using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. These results are used to verify the accuracy of the variational approach that uses a fluid of hard spheres as a reference system, and the relatively high precision of this method is documented. We also show that the energy and pressure cannot be described by the ion-sphere model, which works well under weak screening. The Rosenfeld–Tarazona scaling for the thermal component of excess energy remains applicable, but in a slightly modified form compared with that in the weak-screening regime. The effective inverse-power-law exponent is determined. The excess entropy is evaluated using the variational approach and the MD excess energy data, and a good agreement is demonstrated. These results can be of some interest in the context of complex plasmas and colloidal suspensions as well as for systems in the vicinity of the soft-to-hard interaction crossover in general.
evidence_items.title: Strongly screened Yukawa fluids: Benchmark thermodynamics and the soft-to-hard interaction crossover

evidence_items.summary: Space-based missions such as CoRoT, , and TESS have revolutionised asteroseismology and strengthened its synergies with exoplanet science. With PLATO and ARIEL on the horizon, these synergies will play an even more central role. Kepler We revisit the characterisation of the nearby K dwarf HD 219134 using advanced seismic diagnostics. Our goals are to investigate the reported tension between asteroseismic and interferometric radii, update the fundamental parameters of the star, refine the properties of its planetary system, and investigate the coupled rotational, magnetic, and star–planet evolution of the system, including the atmospheric mass‑loss histories of its planets. The stellar characterisation is based on detailed asteroseismic forward modelling complemented by seismic inversions to quantify systematic uncertainties associated with non‑seismic constraints, assess the compatibility of radius measurements, and evaluate the impact of surface modelling on seismic inferences. The revised stellar properties were used as inputs for rotational evolution investigations, stellar wind modelling, and high‑energy irradiation histories. Seismic inversions rule out the most recent interferometric radius determination, whereas asteroseismic and spectroscopic results are compatible with the previous interferometric measurement from 2019. We derive revised stellar mass, radius, and age of 0.779 ± 0.015 ± 0.006 , M ⊙, 0.753 ± 0.005 ± 0.002 , R ⊙, and 8.92 ± 0.89 ± 0.19 Gyr, respectively. The quoted systematic uncertainties reflect contributions from the non-seismic observational constraints only. Literature values for combined uncertainties arising from physical inputs and surface-effect prescriptions are 0.007M ⊙, 0.002R ⊙, and 0.81 Gyr, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Detailed study of HD 219134: A benchmark K dwarf with a compact planetary system

evidence_items.summary: Active learning promises to reduce annotation cost by letting a model choose which unlabelled examples should be labelled next, but published gains vary widely and some strategies have been reported to perform worse than random selection. This study compares six query strategies under identical conditions on three real image datasets: handwritten digits from MNIST, product photographs from Fashion-MNIST and the smaller UCI Digits collection. Starting from 20 randomly chosen labelled images, a logistic-regression classifier was retrained after each batch of queries until 1,000 images (400 for Digits) had been labelled, with five random seeds per condition. The strategies were random sampling, least-confidence, margin and entropy uncertainty sampling, k-center greedy diversity sampling, and margin sampling combined with k-means diversification of each batch. Margin sampling with batch diversification was the most label-efficient strategy on all three datasets: it reached 95% of the accuracy of a model trained on the full pool with 372, 452 and 82 labels on average, whereas random sampling needed 750 and 216 labels on MNIST and Digits and reached the target in only one of five runs on Fashion-MNIST (at 820 labels), and its area under the learning curve exceeded that of random sampling in all 15 runs. However, least-confidence and entropy sampling were worse than random sampling throughout the budget on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, and k-center greedy sampling ended 16.3 and 9.9 percentage points below random sampling on these datasets. Inspection of the images queried by each strategy explained these failures: entropy sampling repeatedly selected visually similar ambiguous digits from a few classes, whereas k-center greedy selected atypical images, whose distance to their tenth-nearest neighbour was 1.38 and 1.82 times the pool median, and over-sampled particular classes. On the small Digits dataset all strategies outperformed random sampling.
evidence_items.title: When uncertainty sampling backfires: A benchmark of active learning query strategies on real image datasets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) based on Neuroevolution Potential (NEP) models were developed for the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate ([Emim][Ac]) using first-principles reference data generated with four density functionals: PBE-D3, RPBE-D3, optB88-vdW, and SCAN+rVV10. Using a unified training protocol, the resulting NEP models were systematically benchmarked against structural, thermophysical, transport, and hydrogen-bond-network properties, including radial distribution functions (RDFs), coordination numbers, neutron total scattering profiles, density, viscosity, ionic conductivity, and thermal conductivity. Spearman correlation analysis and weighted composite scoring were further used to establish a property-oriented evaluation framework for MLFF assessment and selection. The results reveal a pronounced dependence of NEP performance on the density functional used to generate the reference data. Although all four models reproduce the dominant local structural features of [Emim][Ac], appreciable differences emerge in medium-range structural ordering and transport properties. The PBE-D3-based NEP provides the most accurate overall description of structural properties, whereas the optB88-vdW-based NEP yields the closest agreement with experimental transport properties, particularly viscosity and ionic conductivity. Analysis of the hydrogen-bond network further reveals systematic relationships among hydrogen-bond populations, residence times, free-ion fractions, and ion transport. These results demonstrate that, for [Emim][Ac], the exchange–correlation functional used for reference-data generation influences the physical fidelity and property-specific performance of the resulting NEP models.
evidence_items.title:
Performance of
Neuroevolution Potentials for the Ionic
Liquid [Emim][Ac]: A Systematic Benchmark of Four Density Functionals

evidence_items.summary: Design errors carried over into construction lead to rework, material waste, and avoidable embodied carbon. Rule-based compliance checking in Building Information Modelling (BIM) can identify explicit design issues. However, current rule-based engines struggle to capture complex spatial arrangements and contextual geometric relationships among surrounding components. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising alternative by learning tacit, geometry-dependent conventions of expert practice directly from BIM data. Yet existing AI approaches either learn from 2D representations or rely on handcrafted geometric features that presuppose the target rules. We conduct a controlled study on a parametric benchmark derived from a single apartment plan. A graph transformer predicts where a masked door belongs along a known host wall. It learns from BIM topology and pose-conditioned neural signed distance function (SDF) embeddings, without explicit coordinate features. On unseen rigid transforms, the model achieves 79.1% side accuracy. A graph attention baseline reaches 68.9%, and a message-passing baseline stays at chance. On a second plan with a different topology, it reaches 68.2%. Doubling the training data does not raise this. Without retraining, the first plan’s model reaches 74.0% on the second. Performance on an unseen room-semantic configuration falls to chance. This is a necessary step towards learning tacit design conventions.
evidence_items.title: Recovering Predefined Door-Placement Rules from BIM Geometry: A Controlled Benchmark of Graph Transformers over Neural Signed Distance Function Embeddings

evidence_items.summary: Hospital patient services (registration and appointment scheduling) often face fragmented systems, long handling times, and data-entry errors, while patients expect instant 24/7 digital interactions. This study uses Design Science Research to develop a prescriptive five-phase framework for CRM-integrated agentic AI, whose novelty lies in combining bounded transactional agency, middleware-mediated access to CRM/SIMRS tools, and staged governance. Its design assumptions are evaluated through a controlled proof of concept (PoC). The PoC implements an end-to-end transactional conversational workflow (WhatsApp/web chat) in which an LLM-based agent uses API middleware to call tools on a CRM/SIMRS sandbox, avoiding direct database access. The artefact structures are: preparation and alignment; analysis and detailed design; implementation and controlled testing; pilot and evaluation; and scaling and institutionalization, supported by governance mechanisms (clinical “green/red” boundaries, audit logging, and human-in-the-loop supervision). Empirical evaluation applied black-box testing across 15 positive and negative scenarios comprising 285 executions. Of these, 246 met the predefined scenario criteria, and 39 failed, yielding an overall controlled-scenario success rate of 86.32%. A separate message-level latency log contained 292 message-response pairs across 58 recorded conversation groups; median response time was 9 s (IQR 4–19 s), with 88.70% of responses returned in under 30 s and 97.26% in under 60 s. Selected persisted CRM records were additionally checked through authorized visual inspection, with no discrepancies observed. These findings support technical feasibility under controlled PoC conditions while identifying patient-centred evaluation, cybersecurity assessment, production load testing, economic evaluation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-site validation as requirements for broader deployment.
evidence_items.title: A Prescriptive Design Framework for CRM-Integrated Agentic AI in Hospital Patient Services: Design Science Development and Empirical Proof-of-Concept Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Municipalities increasingly delegate healthcare, social assistance, utilities, transit, and identity verification to semi-autonomous systems. Real-world failures, including Australia's Robodebt scheme and the Dutch childcare benefits scandal, show that automated administration can strip life-sustaining services from large populations whose formal entitlements never changed. Existing governance responses remain fragmented across sectoral silos, with none enforcing a computationally verified constraint at the individual level across multiple domains concurrently. We present \HSC{}, a multi-agent framework that operationalizes essential human functioning as a non-compensatory constraint on automated municipal allocation. The architecture establishes a per-resident capability floor over ten normalized dimensions, identifying deprivation via an Alkire--Foster dual cutoff so that surplus in one domain cannot offset deficits in another. A Human Sovereignty Gate evaluates candidate allocations by measured worst-case capability impact and reversibility, recording commitments in an auditable ledger for which we prove that no admissible sequence of automated decisions can cross the floor. A Basic Needs Assurance Engine coordinates sector agents over a cyclic dependency graph to block cross-sector cascades, backed by an offline resilience reserve during platform outages. We derive a feasibility bound showing that individual risk tolerance cannot be legislated to zero, and specify an agent-based evaluation protocol for 250{,}000 synthetic residents across six disruption scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Human Sovereignty in the Agentic City: Enforcing Multi-Sector Capability Floors Against Automated Deprivation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The increasing digitalization of smart grids exposes cyber-physical infrastructures to sophisticated false-data injection, communication spoofing, and supply-chain attacks, challenging the reliability of conventional intrusion detection under previously unseen operational conditions. Although machine-learning models can identify anomalous patterns, predictive discrimination alone does not establish whether automated decisions are safe, explainable, or operationally accountable. This study introduces GRIDGUARD-AI, an explainable, safety-assured agentic investigation framework integrating random forests (RF), temporal convolutional networks (TCN), and autoencoder (AE)-based anomaly detection with deterministic risk escalation, evidence-grounded AI investigations, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) governance. Using the Data4Cyber dataset, eight-fold leave-one-scenario-out evaluation examines 14,202 rolling windows containing 141 variables across eight operational scenarios. Results reveal substantial cross-scenario variability in detector discrimination, reinforcing the importance of evaluating generalization beyond familiar attack conditions. An exploratory three-way assurance policy classified 1,697 windows as SAFE, 501 as AUTO ALERT, and 12,004 as HUMAN REVIEW. Of 8,455 attack windows, 138 were incorrectly released SAFE (1.63%), yielding 98.37% attack escalation into automatic alert or human review rather than equivalent detection accuracy. Sequential AI-agent investigations completed 24/24 cases after quota-related retries, while automatic tool-calling workflows completed 8/8 scenario probes. Despite demonstrating traceable evidence handling and bounded investigation capabilities, the substantial human-review burden (84.52%), concentrated false-safe failures, and post-hoc policy refinement prevent claims of deployment-ready protection.
evidence_items.title: GRIDGUARD-AI: Scenario-Held-Out Cyberattack Detection with Explainable Assurance and Bounded Agentic Investigation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence agents now search, evaluate, negotiate, and pay on behalf of consumers, while firms deploy agents that create content, personalize offers, and complete transactions. Agentic commerce therefore weakens a foundational assumption of marketing thought and marketing measurement: that the recipient of marketing activity is a human being. The evidence is scattered across marketing, information systems, computer science, economics, and law, and it has a largely forgotten first act in the shopbot research of the late 1990s. Following the SPAR-4-SLR protocol with PRISMA 2020 reporting, we screen 5,157 records from Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO Business Source and add verified snowballing to assemble 140 primary studies spanning 1994 to 2026. Each study is coded on influence direction, customer journey stage, delegation depth, method, and research wave. The synthesis yields an actor taxonomy with a five-level delegation ladder, an influence triad that separates marketing to, through, and by agents, an integrated account of trust and governance infrastructure, and a market-level analysis connecting both research waves. The Agentic Commerce Reference Framework consolidates this evidence into four auditable layers with explicit cross-layer dynamics, a ten-proposition research agenda, and five measurement instruments for analytics practice. A complete replication package accompanies the article.
evidence_items.title: When the customer is a machine: a systematic literature review and integrative framework of agentic commerce

evidence_items.summary: The Deep Hough Transform (DHT) finds straight lines in images by letting a neural network vote on which line each part of the image supports. Lines need only two numbers to describe, so the voting table is small. Curves such as parabolas, circles and ellipses need three to five numbers, and the voting table then grows so fast that it no longer fits in memory. We propose a two-step voting scheme that avoids this. The first step votes only on where the curve is, using a small two-dimensional table. The second step votes on the curve's shape, but only around the few best locations from step one. This cuts memory sharply. Lines are the simple case that needs no second step. The method works when you tell it which curve family to look for. It does not discover shapes on its own. We also introduce a score for how well a detected curve matches the true one, and a synthetic test set of parabolas, circles and ellipses with noise, occlusion and distractor shapes. We compare against RANSAC, a standard curve-fitting method, tuned in the same careful way as our own model, with settings chosen on a validation set and the test set used once. On parabolas, averaged over three runs, our method scores 0.696 with six probe shapes and 0.753 with twelve, against 0.725 for RANSAC. So it is slightly behind with six, and modestly ahead with twelve. On circles and ellipses (one run each) it roughly ties on circles and falls a bit behind on ellipses. We do not claim better accuracy than classical fitting. The advantage is memory: for ellipses, a full voting table with 32 bins on every axis would need about 4 GB, while our method needs 236 KB. That comparison uses a coarser grid for our method. On the same grid, the full table would need about 27 MB, still about 117 times more. Most of the remaining error comes from the first step, finding where the curve is. If we give the second step the true locations, the score rises from 0.71 to 0.94.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Lines: A Factorized Deep Hough Transform for Parametric Curve Detection

evidence_items.summary: Dataset: Multi-facility, high-temporal-resolution phenomics of growth–defence allocation mechanisms in potato — supporting data This dataset provides the cleaned and harmonised phenotyping data underlying the manuscript " Exploration of growth versus defence allocation mechanisms by phenomics tools " (Poque, et al.). The study quantifies growth–defence allocation responses in  Solanum tuberosum  cv. Désirée under pathogen-free conditions using two independent Nordic high-throughput plant phenotyping facilities: the National Plant Phenotyping Infrastructure (NaPPI, University of Helsinki, Finland) and PhenoLab (University of Copenhagen, Denmark). Experimental design Plants were grown in controlled-environment automated conveyor platforms for four weeks (spring 2019 at NaPPI; autumn 2019 at PhenoLab). Three chemical treatment groups were applied to Désirée: untreated control, BABA (β-aminobutyric acid, 10 mM), and potassium phosphite (KPhi/Phosphite, 36 mM Proalexin). Six transgenic potato lines in the Désirée background were also phenotyped: R2A and blb1 (single Rpi genes), 3R1 and 3R2 (three-gene Rpi stack: Rpi-blb1 , Rpi-blb2 , Rpi-vnt1.1 ), and coi1H1 and coi1X5 (RNAi knockdown of the jasmonate co-receptor StCOI1 ). Six biological replicates were used per genotype and treatment.

evidence_items.summary: Dataset Description This dataset provides reference interpretation records and validation results for a remote-sensing assessment of agricultural land detection in Wadi Hadhramaut, Yemen, for the year 2021. The archive includes: Reference classifications for 250 sampled cells. Repeat interpretation records for 51 cells, including the predefined QA50 sample and one additional low-confidence cell. Researcher-approved adjudication records for 14 cases. A technically consolidated 250-cell reference dataset. Sampling information, evaluation weights, and 1,500 prediction records from six candidate classification rules. Recomputed accuracy statistics and supporting documentation for reproducibility. The evaluation demonstrates that high overall classification accuracy (approximately 95.46%) can coexist with low agricultural detection sensitivity (approximately 15.26%), highlighting the limitations of overall accuracy when agricultural areas are rare. Methodological limitations: The reference dataset underwent retrospective technical consolidation. Independent second-interpreter identity was not documented, and the dataset should not be described as independently verified field ground truth. The dataset is intended to support scientific transparency, methodological evaluation, and further research on agricultural remote sensing in hyper-arid environments.
evidence_items.title: Wadi Hadhramaut 2021 Agricultural Support-Rule Evaluation: A 250-Cell Reference Dataset and Validation Results (Version 1.0)

evidence_items.summary: We introduce CARTE (Culturally Anchored Regional-Territorial Evaluation), a multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to discriminate fine grained, geographically grounded and regionally differentiated knowledge within France. While prior benchmarks focus on national-level cultural understanding, they largely overlook intra-country variation and the need to distinguish between closely related regional contexts. CARTE addresses this gap by introducing 3,132 questions spanning the 13 metropolitan regions of France and covering 12 thematic domains, including culture, language, demographics, economy, environment, and mobility. Questions underwent four-stage validation: human review, LLM-as-a-judge, model-based difficulty calibration, and a second human review. We further introduce CARTE-LV, a subset targeting Linguistic Variation across French regions, enabling focused evaluation of language-related differences. We evaluate 32 open-weight LLMs of 1B to 30B parameters and three frontier API models across zero-, one-, and three-shot settings. Our experiments reveal performance disparities across regions and model scales, suggesting systematic gaps in pretraining coverage and limited robustness to intra-national variation.
evidence_items.title: CARTE: A Benchmark for Mapping Language Model Knowledge Across France

evidence_items.summary: The identification and localization of errors is a core task in peer review, yet the exponential growth of scientific output has made it increasingly difficult for human reviewers to reliably detect errors given the limited pool of experts. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support such evaluation tasks, from academic peer review to automated scientific assessment. However, despite the growing use of LLMs in review systems, their capabilities to pinpoint errors remain underexplored. In this work, we introduce Fault Localization Across Writing in Science (FLAWS), an automated benchmark consisting of 713 paper-error pairs designed to evaluate how effectively LLMs detect errors that undermine key claims in research papers. We construct the benchmark by systematically inserting claim-invalidating errors into peer-reviewed papers using LLMs, paired with an automated evaluation metric that measures whether models can identify and localize these errors. Developing such a benchmark presents unique challenges that we overcome: ensuring that the inserted errors are well-defined, challenging, and relevant to the content of the paper, avoiding artifacts that would make identification trivial, and designing a scalable, automated evaluation metric. On the resulting benchmark, we evaluate five frontier LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek Reasoner v3.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT 5, and Grok 4. Among these, GPT 5 is the top-performing model, achieving 39.1% identification accuracy when k=10, where k is the number of top-ranked error text candidates generated by the LLM.
evidence_items.title: FLAWS: A Benchmark for Error Identification and Localization in Scientific Papers

evidence_items.summary: We investigate cross-domain few-shot learning under the constraint that fine-tuning of backbones (i.e., feature extractors) is impossible or infeasible---a scenario that is increasingly common in practical use cases---and show how representing few-shot classification as a series of multiple instance verification (MIV) tasks enables competitive classification performance using the static embeddings produced by frozen, "black-box" backbones. More specifically, based on this novel representation, we introduce a new approach to few-shot domain adaptation named the "MIV-head": a classification head that is backbone-agnostic and computationally efficient. We show that the core components of the MIV-head, when trained on few-shot data from a target domain, collectively yield strong performance on test data from that domain. Importantly, they do so without fine-tuning the backbone, requiring only the "meta-testing" phase. In experiments under various settings on an extension of the Meta-Dataset benchmark for cross-domain few-shot image classification, using representative off-the-shelf convolutional neural network and vision transformer backbones pretrained on ImageNet1K, we demonstrate that the MIV-head achieves highly competitive accuracy when compared to state-of-the-art "adapter" (or "partial fine-tuning") methods applied to the same backbones, while incurring substantially lower adaptation cost. Moreover, compared to our approach, well-known "classification head" approaches achieve a substantially lower level of accuracy. We share our code at: https://github.com/xxweka/MIV-head.
evidence_items.title: Few-shot Classification as Multi-instance Verification: Effective Backbone-agnostic Transfer across Domains

evidence_items.summary: Proactive agents can support group collaboration by surfacing useful information without waiting to be asked, but even relevant contributions can be disruptive if poorly timed. In this work, we isolate the timing question: given a fixed candidate contribution such as a clarification or relevant fact, when should an AI agent chime in? We introduce PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat), to our knowledge the first benchmark with large-scale human judgments of proactive agent timing collected from participants in the same unscripted multi-party conversations they took part in. To collect high-quality judgments, we design a novel interface in which 2-4 people chat synchronously, author candidate AI contribution messages, place their own and others' contributions into the chat history, and then deliberate as a group about the best placement for each message. PITCH contains 384 candidate contributions and 1,091 judgments, each marking an ideal turn, an acceptable window, or that a contribution should not appear, from 89 participants engaged in 35 conversations. Evaluating 15 models across 28 configurations, we find that while models can place contributions well when given the entire conversation history, they systematically chime in too early when asked to decide live as the conversation unfolds: best-turn accuracy falls from 57.8% to 19.0%, with nearly half of placements occurring before every participant's acceptable window. In comparison, lay humans deciding live are more accurate (23.7% vs 19.0%), and fewer of their placements are premature (39.7% vs 46.4%). Model reasoning traces show that 93% of intervention justifications cite relevance, while almost none consider waiting. By providing a human-grounded benchmark, our work reveals gaps in agents' ability to integrate into group settings and points towards proactive agents that can reason explicitly about appropriate timing.
evidence_items.title: When Should AI Chime In? Benchmarking Timely Contribution of Proactive Agents in Multi-Party Chat

evidence_items.summary: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20 Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements? This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model. A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage. The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement.
evidence_items.title: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT  Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology  STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20  Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements?  This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model.  A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage.  The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement.  The proposed minimum experimental prototype uses a closed microfluidic chip with interchangeable handling modules, two independently referenced readout channels, simulated or inert-tracer specimens, a separate audit service, and a physically verifiable stop mechanism. Proposed tests include unauthorized-action challenges, hidden calibration drift, interrupted events, sample contamination, unannounced network partitions, and independent laboratory replay or rerun.  DOI-linked scientific references establish the relevant literature in automated laboratories, microrobotics, quantum sensing, uncertainty metrology, FAIR data stewardship, and computational reproducibility. They do not independently validate the integrated system proposed here.  SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS  This book is a hypothesis-forming nonclinical research architecture. It reports no completed microrobotic or quantum biosensing experiments, no demonstrated clinical performance, no universal quantum advantage, and no autonomous system capable of authorizing itself. Statistical models, formulas, and decision policies require experimental verification, specialized review, and appropriate boundary conditions. A failed external reference, unavailable provenance chain, or revoked permission requires abstention rather than inference by convenience.  STARLI RESEARCH PHILOSOPHY  A trustworthy laboratory must remain answerable to evidence outside itself. Autonomy becomes scientifically meaningful when an experiment can be stopped, questioned, reconstructed, and handed to future researchers who retain the right to refuse its original assumptions.

evidence_items.summary: AUTONOMOUS FAILURE DIAGNOSIS FOR MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING AT THE LIMIT Fault Trees × Measurement Credibility × Verified Safe Stopping STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 18 When a microrobotic sampling platform reports a plausible result, how can researchers determine whether the measurement is trustworthy—and whether the system should have stopped before reporting it? This research monograph investigates the scientific, statistical, and engineering foundations of autonomous failure diagnosis in microrobotic sampling and quantum-enabled biosensing. Rather than treating alarm accuracy as sufficient evidence of reliability, the study examines the entire measurement pathway, from physical actuation and raw detector signals to calibration references, uncertainty estimation, downstream inference, physical interlocks, and independently verifiable release decisions. The 771-page research architecture contains 82 chapters, 410 independently paginated research investigations, 30 interconnected mathematical studies, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Its principal investigations address sensor drift, common-mode reference failure, unknown-fault recognition, multivariate residual monitoring, sequential change detection, actuator latency, optical heating, microfluidic contamination, fault propagation, adversarial experimental design, and verified emergency stopping. A central research proposition is that correlation-aware, multi-source monitoring may reduce the release of corrupted measurements under previously unseen fault conditions compared with conventional fixed-threshold monitoring. The proposed experimental framework emphasizes independent fault injection, blinded evaluation, strong classical measurement comparators, explicit uncertainty accounting, and reproducible nonclinical hardware-in-the-loop testing. Particular attention is given to distinguishing detectable anomalies from identifiable root causes.

The 771-page research architecture contains 82 chapters, 410 independently paginated research investigations, 30 interconnected mathematical studies, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos.  Its principal investigations address sensor drift, common-mode reference failure, unknown-fault recognition, multivariate residual monitoring, sequential change detection, actuator latency, optical heating, microfluidic contamination, fault propagation, adversarial experimental design, and verified emergency stopping.  A central research proposition is that correlation-aware, multi-source monitoring may reduce the release of corrupted measurements under previously unseen fault conditions compared with conventional fixed-threshold monitoring.  The proposed experimental framework emphasizes independent fault injection, blinded evaluation, strong classical measurement comparators, explicit uncertainty accounting, and reproducible nonclinical hardware-in-the-loop testing.  Particular attention is given to distinguishing detectable anomalies from identifiable root causes.  A system may recognize that an observation is unreliable without possessing sufficient evidence to determine whether the underlying problem originates from the robotic actuator, sensing hardware, calibration reference, biological specimen, or data-processing pipeline.  Under such conditions, scientifically responsible operation requires abstention, quarantine, and independently verified stopping rather than unjustified confidence.  The 200 Research Gates introduce falsifiable scientific questions with proposed experimental protocols, measurable outcomes, competing explanations, and explicit rejection conditions.  The 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve provisional research architectures that future investigators may challenge, reconstruct, divide, or replace as stronger evidence becomes available.  DOI-linked scientific literature provides methodological foundations in measurement science, fault detection, microfluidics, microrobotics, quantum sensing, and autonomous laboratory engineering.  Scientific Scope and Limitations  This monograph presents a hypothesis-forming, nonclinical research framework rather than completed experimental findings.  It does not guarantee comprehensive detection of unknown faults, establish autonomous nanoscale clinical systems, prove universal quantum sensing superiority, or authorize medical decisions.  Its proposed methods require independent experimental validation, specialized scientific review, and clearly defined operating boundaries.  STARLI Research Philosophy  A trustworthy autonomous research system must preserve the ability to recognize when its own evidence is insufficient.  Scientific intelligence is not demonstrated solely by producing an answer.  It is also demonstrated by knowing when an answer should be withheld.  By preserving falsifiable questions, physical evidence, uncertainty, and opportunities for independent reconstruction, this monograph invites future human and AI researchers to develop more reliable scientific instruments beyond the assumptions of its original design.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To compare the diagnostic performance of five contemporary vision-enabled large language models (LLMs) in mammography interpretation using a case–control benchmark design. Methods A total of 200 cases were analyzed using a quota-balanced case–control design (100 malignant, BI-RADS 4–5; 100 controls, BI-RADS 1–2). All models (ChatGPT-5T, ChatGPT-5I, ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 2.5 Flash) received standard mammography images. Models were evaluated for lesion detection, laterality, quadrant localization, lesion type, and malignant–benign discrimination. Performance was assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, Cohen’s κ, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Breast density was recorded for all cases, while histopathological subtype and lesion size were documented for malignant cases. Results Lesion detection accuracy ranged from 79% to 91%, with high malignant sensitivity (92%–100%) but lower specificity in normal cases (24%–82%). ChatGPT-5T performed best in laterality (83%; κ = 0.70) and quadrant localization (73%; κ = 0.62). Lesion type classification was modest (74%–85%). In malignant–benign discrimination, ChatGPT-5T achieved the highest balanced accuracy (87%), while ChatGPT-4o showed poor specificity (28%). The study cohort was predominantly composed of lower-density breasts, larger lesions, and invasive ductal carcinoma as the most common subtype. Conclusion Vision-enabled LLMs demonstrated high sensitivity for breast lesion detection and classification tasks. More deliberative models, particularly ChatGPT-5T, consistently outperformed faster counterparts, especially in spatial reasoning tasks. However, reduced specificity in normal cases underscores that current LLM outputs should remain under radiologist supervision as supportive second-reader tools rather than standalone diagnostic systems.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Evaluation of Vision-Enabled Large Language Models in Mammography: A Case–Control Study

evidence_items.summary: Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022--2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.
evidence_items.title: Quant-Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Quantitative Trading Research

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.
evidence_items.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality

evidence_items.summary: Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly 6 times faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a 1.99 times median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark's RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.
evidence_items.title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).
evidence_items.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?

evidence_items.summary: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Claims of quantum advantage in machine learning often rest on classical comparators that lack the same features, on simulation alone, and on unreported hardware cost. QBioBench is a benchmark of quantum machine learning on peripheral biosignals that holds quantum and classical models to the same features and reports calibration and hardware cost. It comprises three clinical tasks, 12-lead ECG diagnosis (PTB-XL), single-lead apnea detection (Apnea-ECG), and wearable stress detection (WESAD), each reduced to six to eight shared dimensions. A factorial grid of projected and fidelity quantum kernels and variational classifiers is screened in noisy simulation, and the promoted configurations are evaluated in an exploratory study on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor on the full test pools of 510 apnea minutes and 512 PTB-XL records. Every prediction is recovered from the device records, intervals resample recordings or patients, and classical baselines are trained on the same units and tested on the same executed inputs. No quantum model reaches its matched support vector machine in ROC-AUC on either primary task, and none is separably better in balanced accuracy. The angle-encoded fidelity and projected kernels reach ROC-AUC 0.697 and 0.693 on apnea, paired differences of $-0.127$ and $-0.119$ to the support vector machine, and both are classical by construction, since the entangling layer of the encoding cancels from the fidelity kernel and leaves closed-form local expectations in the projected kernel. A variational classifier comes closest, reaching 0.797 on apnea (difference $-0.012$, 95\% interval $[-0.052, +0.027]$), and falls to chance without its two-qubit gates. Test sets of the size that circuit budgets favour are unreliable, as random 80-minute subsets of the apnea pool give the fidelity kernel a central 95\% range of ROC-AUC from 0.589 to 0.797. Readout mitigation changed ROC-AUC by at most 0.015.
evidence_items.title: QBioBench: Benchmark of quantum machine learning for peripheral biosignals on real hardware

evidence_items.summary: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.
evidence_items.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D

evidence_items.summary: Neural speech codecs provide discrete tokens for speech generation. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences, but each token must then carry more linguistic and acoustic information. Variable-frame-rate codecs address this trade-off by adapting token allocation to speech content, but threshold-based allocation lets content determine the token count, so the sequence length a speech generator must produce varies across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting. We present RubatoCodec, a variable-frame-rate speech codec built on X-Codec-2 with an exact utterance-level event budget and streaming decoding. Its Adaptive Firing mechanism uses changes in codec features and waveform spectra to divide speech into variable-duration events without a learned boundary predictor. Discrete codes and an explicit duration represent each event, allowing a speech generator to predict and decode one event at a time. Controlled experiments show that adaptive allocation outperforms fixed-rate coding in reconstruction fidelity and intelligibility at low event rates. A model trained on large-scale multilingual speech achieves competitive reconstruction quality across English, Japanese, and Mandarin, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In a matched text-to-speech comparison, the adaptive representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 with comparable speaker similarity. The speech generator also learns the codec's utterance-level event budget without an explicit generation-time rate constraint. These results demonstrate that budgeted adaptive speech representations support both high-quality reconstruction and streaming text-to-speech generation. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec and https://huggingface.co/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec.
evidence_items.title: RubatoCodec: Budgeted Adaptive Speech Tokenization with Streaming Decoding

evidence_items.summary: Despite substantial progress in Deep Search agents, their ability to conduct end-to-end research in real-world open Web environments remains insufficiently evaluated. Unlike static retrieval settings, information on the real-world Web is distributed across diverse sources, modalities, and heterogeneous formats, often involving complex interaction mechanisms that require agents to autonomously search for, access, and integrate relevant evidence during execution. To address this gap, we introduce the OpenDS task, designed to evaluate agents' ability to perform multi-step deep search in the live, open Web. This task requires agents to autonomously explore the real Web, discover and connect relevant evidence from multiple independent sources through Web search, browser interaction, and evidence processing, and ultimately determine a unique factual answer. Building on this task formulation, we construct OpenDS-World, a benchmark comprising 200 challenging tasks spanning diverse information modalities, heterogeneous file formats, and interactive access requirements, with independent human verification to ensure evidence validity and answer uniqueness. We evaluate 12 frontier models under a unified tool environment and execution protocol. The best-performing model achieves 39.0% accuracy, while human evaluation across 1,000 independent attempts yields 21.1% accuracy. Further analyses of tool usage, search cost, termination behavior, and failure recovery reveal substantial differences in research strategies across models, as well as persistent challenges in tool coordination and long-horizon search management. OpenDS-World provides a unified evaluation platform for systematically assessing and advancing agents' autonomous deep search capabilities in real-world open Web environments.
evidence_items.title: Deep Search in Real-World Web Environments

evidence_items.summary: High-quality image editing requires precise modification of target regions while preserving the content of unrelated regions. Existing editing models produce flattened outputs that limit precise local manipulation and layer reuse, while decomposition methods typically optimize layer recovery separately from instruction-driven editing. To this end, we introduce LayerEditor, a unified framework that couples instruction-guided image editing with controllable generation of reusable RGBA layers. At its core, In-Context RGB-Alpha Token Modeling jointly represents the edited canvas and an ordered sequence of RGB-Alpha layers within a single token sequence, enabling semantic edits and explicit control over individual layer content. To retain the pretrained model's editing capability during adaptation to layered outputs, we propose Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation, which transfers its editing prior to both the edited canvas and the image composed from the predicted layers. To support training and evaluation, we construct LayerEditor-100K, a large-scale paired image-editing dataset with ordered RGBA layer annotations, and introduce dedicated benchmarks for layered editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerEditor maintains strong editing fidelity while generating accurate RGBA layers, supporting both flexible layer-level manipulation and multi-layer decomposition.
evidence_items.title: Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Clinical metagenomic sequencing detects hundreds of organisms whose relevance to infection requires clinicians' manual interpretation. We retrospectively reviewed 4,855 specimens from 19 sampling sites, linked 1.33 million detected organisms to clinical culprit-pathogen determinations, and fine-tuned a large language model on these labels. The model recovered 92.44% of reference culprit calls in the held-out test set and 84.49% in a later cohort. In a blinded re-adjudication of 215 cases, the model matched 90.5% of culprit calls on which both expert reviewers agreed. Adjudication accuracy varied with organism identity and specimen types. mNGS-derived metrics such as read counts or genome coverage alone were insufficient to identify culprit pathogens, and organisms classified as common colonizers could still be judged causative. Certain organisms were frequently co-reported as causative in the same specimen. These findings support further evaluation of human and AI-assisted report review, particularly regarding missed pathogens, excess calls, and differences across specimen types.
evidence_items.title: Clinical pathogen adjudication in metagenomic sequencing using a large language model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Introduction Skin cancer is a growing global cause of morbidity and mortality. Rural populations are at an increased risk due to greater ultraviolet exposure and limited access to dermatology services. Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information, their ability to accurately diagnose and triage skin lesions remains uncertain. Objectives To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy, triage safety and reproducibility of multimodal LLMs in interpreting skin lesions representative of rural clinical practice. Methods Seven multimodal LLMs from three developers (OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic) were evaluated using 34 histopathologically confirmed skin lesions from a rural Canadian practice. The dataset comprised paired macroscopic and dermoscopic images of both malignant and non-malignant lesions. Each image was assessed independently a total of five times by each model using a standardized prompt. Results A total of 2,380 model outputs were generated. Diagnostic accuracy varied widely across models (39.4%-72.1%). Claude Opus 4.8 achieved the highest accuracy (72.1%) and the best overall balance of sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility. GPT-5.5 Instant had the lowest specificity and highest over-triage rate, whereas Gemini 3.5 Flash had the lowest sensitivity and highest misclassification rate. Safe triage of malignant lesions ranged from 36% to 87%. Dermoscopic images significantly improved AI performance compared with macroscopic images (OR, 1.65; 95% Cl, 1.30–2.10; p < 0.001). Self-reported diagnostic confidence correlated poorly with model performance, and diagnostic reproducibility across repeated runs was moderate to almost perfect for most models. Conclusions Multimodal LLMs can interpret skin lesion images but are not yet accurate, consistent, or safe for independent diagnosis or triage.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language models for skin lesion diagnosis and triage in rural settings

authors: João Sergio dos Santos Soares Pereira
evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence and agentic systems can redistribute reading, research, synthesis, criticism, drafting, and coordination within courts. This article asks how that redistribution changes judicial cognition and which institutional safeguards are needed to preserve legitimate adjudication. Through an interdisciplinary narrative review and doctrinal analysis, it develops a framework of institutional intelligence anchored in Brazilian National Council of Justice Resolution No. 615/2025, as amended by Resolution No. 674/2026. Five categories organize the argument: institutional cognitive space describes the allocation of cognitive work; artificial adversariality identifies structured internal challenge among agents; the institutional rein integrates controls over delegated autonomy; meaningful human initiative emphasizes the continuing human authority to frame problems and determine purposes; and institutional AI curation describes the competence required to select, validate, contextualize, and reject artificial contributions. Recent research on human–AI collaboration and multi-agent failure qualifies the framework: neither human review nor artificial disagreement guarantees reliability, and short-term performance gains do not establish long-term professional competence. The article distinguishes technical auditability from legal reason-giving and internal agent debate from the parties’ right to be heard. It proposes workflow-level evaluation and an illustrative protocol connecting permissions, source verification, escalation, and responsibility. Its contribution is a judicial governance synthesis, not an empirically validated architecture. Legitimate delegation depends on preserving institutional competence and contestability throughout the production of decisions, rather than relying exclusively on human approval of a final text.
evidence_items.title: From Artificial Intelligence to Institutional Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare relies on diverse mathematical frameworks, yet their contributions to model development, evaluation, interpretability, and clinical translation remain fragmented. This systematic review synthesized the classical and emerging mathematical foundations underpinning healthcare AI and examined major methodological and application trends. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, studies published between January 2016 and June 30, 2026, were identified through systematic searches of Scopus, Google Scholar, and PubMed/MEDLINE, with searches conducted using Harzing’s Publish or Perish v8 where applicable. Bibliometric analysis was performed using VOSviewer, while methodological quality was assessed using an adapted JBI-based framework and AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews. Of 653 records identified, 147 studies met the eligibility criteria. Non-mutually exclusive mathematical-domain coding identified linear algebra in 100/147 studies (68.0%), calculus and optimization in 91/147 (61.9%), and probability and statistics in 79/147 (53.7%), highlighting their roles in data representation, learning, optimization, inference, uncertainty quantification, and validation. A separate mutually exclusive classification of dominant methodological themes identified explainable and trustworthy AI in 24/147 studies (16.3%), statistics and learning theory in 23/147 (15.6%), probability and Bayesian methods in 23/147 (15.6%), calculus and optimization in 19/147 (12.9%), and linear algebra in 15/147 (10.2%). Radiology and medical imaging were the leading healthcare application (24.3%), while classification and diagnosis were the most frequent clinical task (17.1%). Overall, healthcare AI is supported by an interconnected mathematical ecosystem. Emerging approaches, including graph neural networks, Transformers, and quantum machine learning, require stronger external validation, standardized benchmarking, and rigorous evaluation for reliable clinical translation.
evidence_items.title: Mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence in healthcare: a systematic review

organizations: Department of Computer Science, Bayero University, Kano 700006, Nigeria
evidence_items.summary: Background: This systematic review aims to evaluate and synthesize the current research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) models, focusing on their roles, performance, datasets, and evaluation metrics in improving breast cancer detection. Method: A systematic search using the PRISMA guideline was conducted. Four electronic databases (Science Direct, IEEE Explore, SpringerLink, and Scopus) and Google Scholar were searched using specific search strings for online articles published between 2020 and 2024. After applying specified inclusion and exclusion criteria, 91 articles were selected for data extraction, synthesis, and quality assessment. Results: This study reveals that generative AI models are used in breast cancer diagnosis for data augmentation, classification, and segmentation. For data augmentation, GAN has proven to be of highest effectiveness, while transformers have the highest effectiveness in terms of classification and segmentation. This review highlights the growing adoption of various publicly and privately available datasets, which have played a crucial role in training and validating these models. The findings showed the importance of selecting appropriate datasets and metrics to enhance the effectiveness of generative AI models in breast cancer diagnosis. A notable gap identified is the underrepresentation of African populations in the datasets used. Furthermore, the limited applicability of these models in real-world clinical settings is attributed to the lack of explainability. Conclusions: This review provides valuable insights into current practices, identifies existing gaps, and highlights areas for future research, aiming to improve the reliability and applicability of AI-based diagnosis in clinical settings.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Models in Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Systematic Review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Benchmarks often build negatives only from well-annotated entities, leaving parts of the target with zero sampling probability. We write W for the share of a declared target's candidate negatives excluded. Assuming nothing about the excluded region, no strict ordering of two models is identified once W exceeds one half, as in all eight DeepMVP tasks; we therefore report the break-even regional difference that would overturn an observed gain. On reconstructed negatives, a protein-level embedding harmed every task's unsampled region, reversing its gain in seven tasks. The measured regional difference was 2.9–12.8 times the heterogeneity within the sampled region, a reference scale that flagged only two reversals. UPNA-PPI's released negatives omit 73.0% of proteins, and its length-three rule excludes pairs even where every protein keeps partners. Benchmarks should report the target and sampling support at the evaluated unit, and measure part of the excluded region.
evidence_items.title: Constructed negatives determine the population a benchmark can rank over

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The heterogeneity of Point of Interest (POI) taxonomies is a persistent challenge for the integration of urban datasets and the development of location-based services. OpenStreetMap (OSM) adopts a flexible, community-driven tagging system, while Foursquare (FS) relies on a curated hierarchical structure. Here we release an openly available, manually validated benchmark dataset that links 1,205 OSM tags to full FS category paths, from broad thematic groups down to fine-grained labels. By making these two widely used but previously unconnected sources interoperable, the dataset enables consistent, multi-scale analyses of urban functions and can be downloaded and reused as a high-precision resource. The dataset is complemented by an automatic alignment procedure, combining text embeddings with LLM-based refinement, whose code we release to support scalable updates of the benchmark as OSM evolves. Together, these elements provide both a robust reference resource and a practical tool for the community. The benchmark is manually curated and validated to serve as a high-quality gold-standard reference, with direct applications to urban analytics, mobility studies, and smart city services.
evidence_items.title: An openly available OpenStreetMap-to-Foursquare category benchmark for points of interest

evidence_items.summary: Abstract New earthquake forecasting models are increasingly reported to outperform established models such as the epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) model. However, the scientific meaning of such improvements depends critically on how the benchmark is constructed. I use the term “under-implemented ETAS” for a benchmark that is unnecessarily restricted, weakly optimized, or otherwise disadvantaged, and propose the Parity of information, Optimization, Generality, and Assessment (POGA) test as a simple framework for assessing model comparisons. The purpose is not to protect ETAS from competition, but to ensure that improvements over established models are scientifically interpretable. A strong benchmark makes victory harder, but also reveals what a new model has genuinely learned that its competitor could not.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating New Earthquake Forecasting Models: Against a Strong ETAS Benchmark, Not an Underimplemented One

evidence_items.summary: Cell defects in photovoltaic (PV) modules directly affect production yield, making early and reliable detection critical. Electroluminescence (EL) imaging is widely used for this purpose since it reveals defects such as microcracks and inactive regions; however, manual assessment is time-consuming and subjective. In this study, EL images from the public ELPV benchmark dataset are automatically classified into four defect-severity levels (flawless, low, medium, high). The proposed method augments a ResNet50 backbone with the Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) block, which adaptively recalibrates channel-wise features. The model is compared against ResNet50, MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetB0 baselines using ImageNet pretrained weights and stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The proposed SE-ResNet50 outperforms all baselines with 0.7609 accuracy and 0.559 macro-F1. Furthermore, an ordinal error-magnitude analysis shows that the SE block yields the smallest and closest errors, reducing the mean absolute level error to 0.443. Nevertheless, the contribution of SE remains limited for the minority 'medium' class, indicating that class imbalance is the principal bottleneck.
evidence_items.title: Photovoltaic Cell Defect Severity Classification with Squeeze-and-Excitation Enhanced ResNet50 on the ELPV Benchmark Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Accepted population displacements provide directional information that can be reused in subsequent derivative-free search. This paper develops the Good Point Set and Trend-Aware Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm (GT-SBOA), combining a dimension-admissible number-theoretic initialization with an auxiliary search direction formed from individual and population-center motion. The auxiliary update is applied to the worse-performing half of the population in every complete sweep, with all objective calls charged to a common evaluation budget. Evaluation covers 29 CEC2017 functions, a two-component ablation, directional-weight sensitivity, and five OR-Library portfolio instances. In the comparison at D=30, GT-SBOA has a mean rank of 2.4138 across eleven algorithms, with 14 lowest mean errors and a significant win/tie/loss record of 16/4/9 against SBOA. The four-method comparison places it first at D=50 and third at D=100, showing that the aggregate advantage is dimension-dependent. The portfolio evaluation retains native initialization in the complete-method comparison and uses GD and IGD to assess frontier accuracy and coverage, with a common-initialization control against the parent algorithm. These comparisons delimit the conditions under which displacement-guided updates offer useful search information within a fixed evaluation budget.
evidence_items.title: A Secretary Bird Optimizer with Good Point Set Initialization and Trend-Aware Search for Benchmark and Portfolio Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Eligibility rules define which interactions contribute to a benchmark score. The low-bias BindingDB benchmark retains a drug only when it has both positive and negative labels, excluding measured inactive pairs involving drugs without a measured active. We reconstructed this rule in a declared BindingDB population and evaluated retained and excluded negatives against the same positive reference. After cleaning and an additional connectivity-overlap restriction, the excluded region contained 78.4% of the measured negative pairs. DrugBAN and MolTrans were trained in three evaluation designs with five seeds; a released BioT5 checkpoint was evaluated on its published split. Across these evaluations, pooled AUROC was 0.072–0.136 lower on excluded negatives. Lower performance also occurred within proteins with sufficient observations in both regions. DrugBAN remained ahead of MolTrans, but the change in their advantage depended on aggregation: it generally increased under pooled AUROC, whereas equalprotein weighting produced smaller or oppositely directed changes. Cross-protein comparisons accounted for approximately 99.8–99.9% of pooled AUROC's pair-comparison weight. The closer BioT5–DrugBAN comparison additionally depended on scoring convention. These results measure regional performance differences, conditional on the chosen positive reference; they do not estimate a causal filter effect or deployment performance. Benchmark reports should specify eligibility, coverage at the evaluated unit, metric aggregation, and performance on excluded regions where labels are available.
evidence_items.title: What a low-bias filter leaves out: measured performance on the excluded negatives of a drug–target interaction benchmark

evidence_items.summary: The increasing replacement of synchronous generation by converter-interfaced photovoltaic (PV) plants introduces new challenges to the output-only modal identification in modern power systems. Besides reducing system inertia, converter dynamics modify the spectral characteristics of measured responses through fast control loops and control-induced interactions, redistributing modal energy and reducing the physical interpretability of conventional identification methods. This paper investigates the impact of converter-induced spectral contamination on two output-only modal identification techniques: classical Prony analysis and Total Least Squares–Estimation of Signal Parameters via Rotational Invariance Techniques (TLS-ESPRIT). Time-domain responses are obtained from the Kundur two-area benchmark system, where one synchronous generator is replaced by a utility-scale PV plant modeled using the standardized WECC dynamic models REGC A, REEC A and REPC A. A fully synchronous reference case together with constant active-power and constant voltage-control operating modes is comparatively analyzed. To complement conventional reconstruction-based metrics, this work proposes the Physical Energy Relevance(PER) metric, which quantifies the fraction of identified modal energy associated with physically relevant dynamic phenomena through a frequency-dependent weighting function. Because PER does not require prior knowledge of the expected modal spectrum, it provides a flexible framework for evaluating the physical significance of output-only modal decompositions. The results show that, although Prony provides accurate reconstruction under synchronous conditions, converter-induced spectral contamination progressively shifts the modal energy toward high-frequency components with limited physical relevance. In contrast, TLS-ESPRIT consistently preserves the concentration of modal energy within the dominant electromechanical frequency bands.
evidence_items.title: Physical Energy Relevance for Output-Only Modal Identification Under Converter-Induced Spectral Contamination in Power Systems
