evidence_items.summary: Designing molecules with prescribed properties is central to pharmaceutical and materials innovation, but vast chemical design spaces make development lengthy and costly. Generative artificial intelligence can accelerate molecular discovery, but its deployment in many real-world domains remains limited by the need for large task-specific training datasets. To enable generative design when property-labeled data are scarce, we present a data-efficient foundation-model adaptation strategy combining complementary positive and negative property prompts with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Generated molecules are then ranked by molecular graph-kernel Gaussian process regression for structure-aware prioritization. In a controlled computational setting, the platform generated candidates with novel scaffolds satisfying multiple design objectives, including predicted target binding, synthesizability, and drug-likeness. Although only a few hundred training molecules per target met all three criteria, the model generated thousands of new molecules matching the desired profiles. For prospective validation, we applied the model to nanoparticle design, a domain of high clinical potential but limited excipient diversity. Fine-tuning on only 1,521 labeled drug-excipient pairs - including just 139 nanoparticle-forming examples identified new nanoparticle-forming excipients for the anticancer drug sorafenib. The model proposed lithocholic acid and the sorafenib metabolite M6, and experiments confirmed that both form stable sorafenib nanoparticles with high encapsulation efficiency and increased in vitro potency. These findings show that foundation-model fine-tuning with complementary prompts and graph-based prioritization enables data-efficient molecular design in low-data chemical domains.
evidence_items.title: Data-efficient molecular and nanoparticle design via fine-tuned large language models

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is credited with teaching reasoning models to write {wait} before reconsidering a step, yet large RL accuracy gains do not require the word. This view can confuse what RL discovers with what a model inherits from its training data. We trace the word through open models' training histories, reading it with label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage and an injected-error test, all computed from sampled outputs. We find that zero-RL almost never coins the marker: on bases that lack the word, RL raises MATH-500 accuracy substantially while {wait} stays near absent. It arrives with training data: mid-training in OLMo-3, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces installs it in most models whose base lacks it. Where the base already uses it, both released RL-Zero recipes (OLMo-3, MiMo) multiply it, whereas KL-free GRPO from the same base does not; OLMo-3's recipe wears down its form and makes it a more sensitive but more liberal alarm; RL after supervised fine-tuning barely changes it, and our GRPO recipe erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning. Finally, we show that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning and caution against LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics, as automated judges can reverse human-labelled trends.
evidence_items.title: Inherited, Not Invented: Tracing the Provenance of Wait in Reasoning Models

evidence_items.summary: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
evidence_items.title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.
evidence_items.title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
evidence_items.title: RealMe: Immersive Volumetric Video from Minimal Captures

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use

evidence_items.summary: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.
evidence_items.title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles

evidence_items.summary: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.
evidence_items.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift

evidence_items.summary: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
evidence_items.title: Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields ΔSR=0 despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera L_2 and Gaussian blur L_1 both yield ΔSR=0.188, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.
evidence_items.title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).
evidence_items.title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
evidence_items.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as π_{0.5}, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of π_{0.5}, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a 10times smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
evidence_items.title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.
evidence_items.title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data

evidence_items.summary: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.
evidence_items.title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation

evidence_items.summary: Single-instrument automatic music transcription (AMT) has advanced substantially, yet choral applications require soprano, alto, tenor, and bass (SATB) to be transcribed as separate parts. Recent note-level choral AMT instead produces a single merged note track, limiting rehearsal, education, and score reconstruction. To address this limitation, we introduce Part-aware Choral Transcription (PawCT), to our knowledge the first end-to-end neural framework that identifies active SATB parts from choral audio and transcribes each into a separate note-level track. PawCT combines part-specific onset, offset, and frame prediction with part-presence estimation, union-level supervision, and structured training targets using a range prior (RP) based on SATB pitch ranges and its ordered-continuity (OC) extension, which adds within-part melodic continuity and cross-part pitch ordering. On YouChorale, PawCT-RP-OC achieves a macro part-aware note F1 of 0.225 at a 50-ms onset tolerance, outperforming an adapted choral baseline (0.165) by 36.4% relative and a two-stage post-hoc assignment pipeline (0.175). Its part-agnostic variant, PagCT, achieves a 50-ms onset F1 of 0.382, compared with 0.237 for the previous state-of-the-art choral AMT model. Cross-dataset evaluations on CSD and Cantoria further assess performance under dataset shift. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly modeling note transcription and vocal-part assignment. Code and demos are available at https://hanyu-meng.github.io/Paw_Choral_AMT_Demo/.
evidence_items.title: Toward Part-Aware Choral Transcription with singing voice assignment

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Privacy concerns represent a primary barrier to the adoption of large language model (LLM) applications, particularly in sensitive domains such as health care. Although a growing body of survey-based research has examined user privacy concerns with LLMs, no standardized instrument exists for measuring this construct. Objective This study aimed to develop and validate a concise, standardized questionnaire for assessing user privacy concerns with LLM-based systems, suitable for use by researchers and practitioners such as AI application developers and health care professionals. Methods A literature review was conducted to identify privacy-related domains relevant to LLM use. A draft questionnaire was developed and subjected to content validity review by 8 experts. The finalized instrument was administered via Qualtrics to adults aged 18 years or older who were aware of LLM-based applications, recruited through the University of Pittsburgh, LinkedIn, and the Pitt+Me research participant registry between April 2025 and July 2026. Internal consistency reliability and factor structure were assessed, with factor structure examined in a split-sample design, in which exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted on a random one-third of the sample and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) on the holdout two-thirds. Results All questionnaire items achieved acceptable content validity (item-level content validity index >0.80; average scale-level content validity index=0.964). A total of 603 responses were collected. After preprocessing, the final sample comprised 361 participants. Most participants were younger than 35 years of age (198/361, 54.8%), female (230/361, 63.7%), and White (285/361, 78.9%); 88.1% (318/361) held at least a bachelor’s degree. The 6-item questionnaire showed high internal consistency (Cronbach α=0.90; McDonald ω=0.90). EFA (n=121) supported a single dominant factor with all standardized loadings ≥0.70.
evidence_items.title: Development and Validation of the Large Language Model Privacy Concern Assessment Questionnaire: Psychometric Evaluation Study on a Brief Instrument for Assessing User Privacy Concerns With Large Language Model Applications

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The massive volume of paired microbiome and metabolome measurementsgenerated through high-throughput sequencing and mass spectrometryhas created an urgent need for dedicated, integrative analytical pipelines. Existing tools lack the capacity to simultaneously support sample clustering, multi-omics visualization, disease risk stratification, and biological age quantification using matched dual-modal datasets. To overcome this analytical bottleneck, we introduce the matrix factorization with shared and specific graph learning (MFSSG) toolkit: an unsupervised matrix factorization framework that jointly learns both shared and modality-specific graph structures. MFSSG preserves cross-omics spatial consistency by leveraging shared nearest-neighbor graphs derived from analytical profiles and incorporates two complementary regularization termsentropy regularization to enhance cluster discriminability and a pre-trained microbial graph Laplacianto mitigate measurement bias inherent in microbiome sequencing versus metabolomic mass spectrometry data. Validated across three independent multi-omics cohorts derived from gastric and gut biospecimensincluding gastric cancer, end-stage renal disease, and type 1 diabetesMFSSG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art integration methods in disease classification. Furthermore, a novel pairwise learning module enables parallel and accurate quantification of the metabolic age and microbial age, facilitating refined patient risk stratification. This versatile toolkit provides a robust chemometric strategy for uncovering latent biological patterns embedded within heterogeneous multi-omics analytical data.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Enhanced MFSSG Enables Effective and Accurate Integration Analysis for Microbiome−Metabolome Data

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) may support healthcare workforce allocation, but their decisions can be sensitive to demographic cues and decision architecture. This study examined gender–task congruity, Candidate-A dependence under the tested decision architecture, and patient-gender-conditioned nursing allocation. Methods: Three provider-specific LLM configurations were audited across 24 nursing tasks. Male and female nurses were professionally equivalent and counterbalanced across Candidate A/B; patient gender was varied in six intimate-care tasks. Sixty conditions were repeated three times per model, yielding 540 valid outputs. Results: Male nurses were selected in 50.0% of Technical/Procedural and Relational/Educational allocations. Candidate A was selected in all 288 observations, although 285 (99.0%) assigned identical suitability scores. Because A/B assignment was bundled with labeling, presentation order, evaluation order, and response-template anchoring, this pattern indicates Candidate-A dependence under the tested decision architecture rather than an isolated position effect. Changing patient gender from female to male produced 57 female-to-male nurse switches and no reverse switches (p < 0.001). Conclusions: The audited configurations showed no generalized gender–task pattern but demonstrated decision-architecture dependence and patient-gender-conditioned allocation. Fairness audits should assess equivalent-candidate handling, patient preference, and counterfactual stability.
evidence_items.title: Decision-Architecture Dependence and Patient-Gender-Conditioned Allocation in Large-Language-Model-Assisted Nursing Allocation: A Multi-Model Counterfactual Audit

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background Retrieving MRI safety conditions for implanted devices is increasingly complex and time‐consuming. Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of internet‐enabled large language model (LLM) chatbots in retrieving implant‐specific MRI safety conditions, using manufacturer documentation as the reference standard. Study Type Prospective comparative evaluation in a constructed device cohort, followed by a retrospective clinical pilot. Population Fifty purposively selected device configurations and 20 patients (10 with cardiac and 10 with noncardiac devices) referred to the MRI Safety Committee. Field Strength No field‐strength or sequence restrictions. Assessment Standardized single‐shot prompts requested eight parameters from ChatGPT‐5.0, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5: MRI safety label, field strengths, eligible regions/centering, transmit‐coil restrictions, RF exposure limits, maximum spatial gradient, maximum gradient slew rate, and scan duration. Two radiologists (10 and 25 years' experience) and an MRI technologist (32 years) independently scored 1200 parameter‐level outputs against manufacturer Instructions for use and technical manuals using a 5‐point scale (5, fully correct; 1, substantively incorrect or fabricated); scores of 4–5 indicated accuracy. In the pilot, 160 outputs from ChatGPT‐5.6, a newer version of the best‐performing chatbot, were scored identically. Statistical Tests Intraclass correlation coefficient; Gwet's first‐order agreement coefficient (AC1); Friedman test; Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests; device‐clustered bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs); two‐sided significance threshold, p < 0.05. Results Mean ordinal scores were 4.76 (ChatGPT), 4.20 (Gemini), and 4.17 (Claude); ChatGPT scored significantly higher. Respective pooled parameter‐level accuracies were 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89–0.98), 0.79 (0.71–0.86), and 0.78 (0.69–0.87). Pilot accuracy with ChatGPT‐5.6 was 0.98 (95% CI, 0.94–1.00).
evidence_items.title:
Accuracy of Large Language Model Chatbots in Retrieving
                    <scp>MRI</scp>

evidence_items.summary: Safety-aligned language models often encode that a request is harmful yet still comply with it. We turn this gap between internal recognition and observable behavior into an inference-time defense. The proposed activation-steering method uses a multiplicative operator that amplifies the residual-stream component along a harm-recognition direction. Intervention strength scales with the model’s own assessment of the request. A second additive term steers activations along the refusal direction when harm is not internally recognized. Two linear probes computed from the model’s activations gate both components. The model weights remain unchanged, and inference requires neither fine-tuning nor calls to an external model. An external safety classifier is used only before deployment to provide training targets for the second probe. We evaluate five models from three families, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and Mistral-7B-Instruct, in BF16 and NF4. Successful attacks on SORRY-Bench decrease by 40 to 68%. Without hyperparameter retuning, the method removes 67 to 79% of the harmful responses on HarmBench. MMLU accuracy decreases by at most 0.7 percentage points, while over-refusal on lexically hazardous benign prompts increases by 4 to 8 points. Steered NF4 models produce 36 to 62% fewer harmful responses than their unmodified BF16 counterparts.
evidence_items.title: Amplifying Latent Safety in Large Language Models via Gated Activation Steering

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Legal epidemiology is a growing field wherein researchers examine the effects of health policies on health outcomes. Policy surveillance is a key part of the legal epidemiology process and leads to the creation of a legal dataset for econometric analyses. Policy surveillance includes conceptualizing the research scope, collecting legal data, and coding data to answer legal questions. Historically, policy surveillance has been slow and time-consuming, limiting timely information about the effects of health policies on health outcomes. Researchers are exploring the role of artificial intelligence using large language models (LLMs) to increase the efficiency and quality of the policy surveillance process. In this commentary, we describe potential uses of LLMs by researchers conducting policy surveillance as well as potential challenges that will need to be addressed before LLMs are widely used in the process. We also suggest areas for future research, while emphasizing the need for development of guidelines for LLM use in policy surveillance.
evidence_items.title: Commentary: Can large language models improve the quality and efficiency of health policy surveillance?

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: Surgical specialities like plastic and hand surgery, which depend on precision, aesthetic, and functional outcomes, are integrating AI, creating potential and challenges. AI is rapidly transforming clinical procedures, requiring evaluation of its potential to improve clinical care and the challenges it faces. This narrative review critically evaluates the clinical applications, emerging innovations, and ethical challenges of AI in plastic and hand surgery, synthesising evidence on both its transformative potential and the challenges it presents.Method: We conducted a narrative review of peer-reviewed literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (2018-2025). Keywords included “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “plastic surgery,” “hand surgery,” “microsurgery,” and “convolutional neural networks.” We included studies on clinical applications, technological innovations, and ethical considerations. This review differs from existing syntheses by providing a balanced “Potential vs Provocation” framework that systematically addresses both benefits and challenges while proposing concrete implementation strategies for clinical practice.Results: AI technologies such as convolutional neural networks and large language models classify skin lesions, evaluate aesthetics, and automate operative documentation.Conclusion: Innovations such as generative AI, mixed reality, and predictive analytics in microsurgical procedures, patient-specific simulations, and smart rehabilitation have driven tremendous advances in this field. Despite this potential, significant challenges remain, including data bias, limited AI model interpretability, and concerns about liability and privacy. AI in plastic and hand surgery has significant potential to strengthen surgeons; however, integrating it requires acceptance, education, interdisciplinary collaboration, and ethical guidelines to address the challenges of this technological evolution.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Plastic and Hand Surgery – Potential or Provocation?

evidence_items.summary: Abstract As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into aesthetic medicine, its influence on beauty standards and clinical practice warrants closer evaluation, especially among a diverse population. This study aimed to evaluate whether AI-based facial attractiveness platforms assign differing attractiveness scores across ethnic groups despite standardized image characteristics, with the hypothesis that significant differences would exist between ethnic groups and AI platforms, reflecting potential preferential scoring patterns favoring Eurocentric facial features. Cross-sectional comparative study evaluating AI-generated facial attractiveness scores across ethnic groups using multiple AI-based rating platforms. A database of 120 stock AI-generated images of women from diverse ethnic backgrounds (Black, White, Latino, and Asian) was developed from an online platform, with 30 photos per ethnicity. Images were of young adult women in frontal view with neutral expressions. These photographs were then evaluated using five different AI-based facial rating websites: Prettyscale (PS), Attractivenesstest (AT), Beautyscoretest (BST), Hotchat3000 (HC), and Attractivenessscore. White females received the highest average score (8.18), followed by Asian (7.79), Latino (7.72), and Black (6.91). Among AI-based platforms, PS yielded the highest scores (8.50), while BST yielded the lowest (6.65). Post hoc pairwise comparisons indicated significant differences in attractiveness scores between certain ethnicities, such as White versus Black (+ 1.27, p < 0.001), White versus Asian (+ 0.39, p = 0.05), and White versus Latino (+ 0.46, p < 0.001). Pairwise differences in attractiveness scores between AI-based platforms were also significant, such as PS versus BST (+ 1.85, p < 0.001), PS versus AT (+ 0.38, p = 0.007), and PS versus HC (+ 1.54, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that some AI platforms may exhibit bias toward White females.
evidence_items.title: Exploring Racial Bias in Rating Facial Attractiveness Among Artificial Intelligence Platforms

evidence_items.summary: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new opportunities in literary learning, particularly in developing creative writing skills at the elementary school level. This study aims to develop and evaluate a poetry writing learning model based on Poem Generator, named GEN-POEM, as an innovative approach to creative literacy. The research design employed a descriptive qualitative approach within an early-stage research and development framework (define–design–develop). Research subjects involved eight fifth-grade teachers at SD Muhammadiyah 9 "Panglima Sudirman" in Malang City. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions (FGD), and document analysis, then analyzed using thematic analysis techniques. The results indicate that GEN-POEM has a systematic learning syntax comprising orientation, idea exploration, initial drafting, AI integration through Poem Generator, revision and reflection, and presentation of works. Teachers assessed the model as practical, creative, and aligned with 21st-century learning needs, particularly in motivating students and integrating digital technology into literary literacy. Challenges include students' readiness to use AI, instructional time allocation, and the teacher's role as facilitator. Based on teacher feedback, GEN-POEM was refined to enhance flexibility and effectiveness. This study contributes to the development of digital creative literacy theory while offering practical implications for elementary school teachers in integrating AI into learning. From a policy perspective, these findings support the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum and the national digital literacy agenda. A limitation of this study is that its subjects were limited to teachers; further research is therefore recommended to test the direct implementation of GEN-POEM with students in the classroom.
evidence_items.title: GEN-POEM Model Innovation: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Poetry Writing Instruction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Simulation-based controller comparisons can report a single winner even when score differences are too small to justify a unique engineering preference. We assessed preference reliability for five fixed controllers on a numerically verified nonlinear rotary inverted pendulum model using two independent Latin-hypercube realizations across matched ± 10%, ± 15%, and ± 20% uncertainty bands (30,000 closed-loop simulations). A four-metric score and a prespecified 5% practical margin quantified controller separation. Under the common uncertainty score, PID had the lowest controller robustness index in every band, but the four leading indices remained within 3.87%. In the pooled ± 15% domain, all ten paired comparisons were detectable after Holm correction, yet 69.40% of 2,000 scenario blocks lacked a unique practical preference. PID retained rank one in 99.95% of paired-bootstrap replicates but only 63.16% and 43.06% under two weight-variation analyses. Post-review sensitivity analyses showed that the principal practical-separation conclusion was robust to the tested CRI coefficient, realization-specific median normalization, and heavier-tail dependence models, while command delay altered separation among near-tied controllers. These findings are specific to the fixed controller portfolio, score definition, RIP model, and simulated uncertainty domain.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying controller preference reliability under uncertainty in a rotary inverted pendulum benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Published database comparisons typically cover engine pairs, conflate the engine effect with the schema effect, and compare queries that do not compute the same result. We present StreamCart, a benchmark built on a realistic e-commerce workload, and use it to decompose performance across six systems, PostgreSQL as an optimized relational baseline and five specialized engines (MongoDB, Cassandra, Neo4j, Elasticsearch, TimescaleDB), each implemented at a naive migration level and at an engine-optimized level, eleven configurations in all. Result equivalence for the claim-bearing analytics queries is verified row by row against the relational reference. Across seven read query classes, no naive implementation outperforms the baseline on any query, and no single engine dominates, with the classes splitting between PostgreSQL, optimized Elasticsearch, and optimized MongoDB. Schema design emerges as a factor on par with engine choice, improving performance by up to 3892 times on Cassandra and 137 times on Elasticsearch, where load-time denormalization lets the optimized form outperform PostgreSQL by 15.8 and 6.3 times on identical results, while a single omitted uniqueness constraint reduced Neo4j write throughput a hundredfold. Concurrent write throughput spans roughly two orders of magnitude (165 to 12,603 events per second). All code, data, and raw timings are public.
evidence_items.title: Decomposing Engine and Schema Effects in Database Performance: A Result-Equivalent E-Commerce Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Modern technological society is highly vulnerable to extreme geomagnetic storms, yet the terrestrial upper limit of such events remains poorly constrained because continuous instrumental geomagnetic records cover only a relatively short historical period. To extend this baseline, we quantitatively reconstruct the geomagnetic superstorm of September 1770 (termed Qianlong XXXV storm) using systematically documented auroral observations preserved in Chinese regional chronicles. These historical records indicate that the auroral oval expanded to a magnetic latitude as low as 20.40°N at the ionospheric height, implying an exceptionally intense magnetospheric disturbance. From this equatorward auroral boundary, we derive a best-estimate Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) index of −1,319 nT (95% Confidence Interval (CI): [−1,832, −1,066]), exceeding the reconstructed Dst intensity of the 1859 Carrington event ( ≈ −1,025 nT, 95% CI of [−1367, −853]) by approximately 30%. An extreme value statistical model suggests an order-of-magnitude recurrence interval of approximately 14,000 years for the Qianlong XXXV event, compared with approximately 1,400 years for Carrington-class storms. These results suggest that the Qianlong XXXV geomagnetic storm represent an important low-latitude benchmark for extreme solar–terrestrial disturbances. This potential benchmark provides a quantitatively constrained reference for testing the physical limits of modern infrastructure and the atmosphere of the Earth under the impact of catastrophic space weather.
evidence_items.title: The Qianlong XXXV event: a potential benchmark for extreme geomagnetic storms based on historical Chinese auroral archives

evidence_items.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative Agentic AI) models, such as Large Language Models (LLMs), and agentic AI have recently gained widespread attention in both research and industry. They have rapidly emerged as a concept that elevates Generative Agentic AI from passive text generators to the next generation of agentic AI as autonomous, goal-driven agents capable of perception, planning, and dynamic action execution—Coherent Generative Agentic AI (CGA). In addition, CGA provides supervisory intelligence by maintaining persistent, evolving internal world models of the environment, networks, resources, agents, user intents, and policies. CGA reasons over time, runs long-horizon plans, checks consequences against its internal models, and coherently orchestrates lower-level controllers. It sits above network controllers, providing a global, semantic, model-driven brain. The paper starts with a review of CGA functional and non-functional characteristics in the context of key research and development results of agentic AI. It introduces a coherence-first architectural construct and system variable across all future 6G/7G networking planes (data-, transport-, management and operations,- orchestration,- autonomicity-, programmability-, and AI as a Service-plane). It proposes a new deterministic CGA mathematical (CGAM) model that provides a new abstraction and theoretical foundation for analyzing the systemic consequences of different structural design and optimization options. It defines the relation between coherence and intelligence. The CGAM model represents the compute–communications continuum as a partially observable, intent-driven, contract-governed, multi-agent dynamical system with persistent memory and coherence constraints. We also included detailed CGAM validation and evaluation measures. This paper explores and details the CGAM’s role in 6G and 7G networking, as well as the challenges and opportunities for future work they present.
evidence_items.title: Coherent Generative Agentic AI Enabled 6G/7G Networking

organizations: Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
evidence_items.summary: Agentic coding tools, such as OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor, are changing how software is developed. These AI-powered systems function as autonomous teammates capable of planning and executing complex development tasks. Agents have become active participants in refactoring, a key practice for improving internal code quality without altering observable behavior. Despite their increasing adoption, there is little empirical understanding of how agentic refactoring is used in practice, how it compares to human-driven refactoring, and what impact it has on code quality. To address this empirical gap, we present a large-scale study of AI agent-generated refactorings in real-world open-source Java projects, analyzing 51,412 refactoring instances across 12,256 pull requests and 14,998 commits based on the AIDev dataset. Our empirical analysis shows that refactoring is a common and intentional activity in this development paradigm, with agents explicitly targeting refactoring in 26.1% of commits. The subsequent analyses of refactoring types, purposes, and code quality focus on the 3,907 commits (32,611 instances) with explicit refactoring intent. Analysis of refactoring types reveals that high-level refactorings form the largest category overall. However, agentic refactoring contains a slightly larger share of lowlevel, consistency-oriented edits than human refactoring (27.6% vs. 24.4%), and its two most frequent operations are Rename Variable (7.6%) and Change Variable Type (6.8%). Additionally, the stated motivations behind agentic refactoring focus overwhelmingly on internal quality concerns (with 52.5% in maintainability and 28.1% in readability), although the measured metric improvements from these frequently occurring low-level refactorings remain limited.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Refactoring: An Empirical Study of AI Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: The high rate at which telecommunication services are changing has yielded a volume of heterogeneous data never seen before such as call detail records, signaling data, and subscriber activity traces. These datasets are crucial in relation to optimization and business intelligence, but effective use of such datasets requires quality metadata. Traditional metadata management is mostly manual and centralized, which cannot support the pace and scale of the new telecom big data systems. As a solution to these shortcomings, the present article suggests a scalable metadata mining strategy that is founded on agentic intelligence. In comparison to more traditional machine learning pipelines, agentic intelligence enables the use of autonomous goal-oriented AI agents, capable of reasoning in a hard data space and relevant to new network topologies and network schemas. The proposed architecture will include a multiagent architecture at a distributed level, having specialized agents: (1) schema drifting ingestion and monitoring agents of data flows; (2) semantic mining actors based on natural language processing to infer contextual metadata; (3) process-aware agents for process mining to determine lineage and dependencies between data; and (4) compliance with policy and metadata retrospect: government agents. A major effect of the work is the integration of agentic intelligence and scalable infrastructures of big data such as cloud-native analytics platforms and distributed data lakes. These agents coordinate themselves using lightweight coordination mechanisms to provide a persistent metadata knowledge layer that facilitates system interoperability and robust downstream analytics. The design concepts are geared toward horizontal scalability and fault tolerance, enabling the distribution of the agents at dynamically evolving manner regarding the workload peak. Besides, agents also enhance their strategies upon continuous feedback to handle concept drift as well.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Intelligence for Scalable Metadata Mining in Telecom Big Data Systems

evidence_items.summary: Bringing a new drug to market can exceed $1 billion, and integrated commercial computational-chemistry platforms cost $200,000–$5,000,000 per year, placing them beyond most resource-constrained research groups. We demonstrate that open-source tools with large language model (LLM) orchestration can democratize early-stage New Chemical Entity (NCE) prioritisation. Three computational case studies (Case A: proprietary target, class withheld, public experimental co-crystal structure; Case B: kinase with co-crystal structure; Case C: protein–protein-interaction interface, apo) each ran Tier 1 (target-enriched ZINC20 library) and Tier 2 (GNINA v1.1 docking with CNN rescoring, plus SwissADME and ADMETlab 2.0 profiling). Tiers 3–4 are proposed future work. A tiered Claude Opus 4/Sonnet 4 agent orchestrated the workflow. Each library (~154,000–400,000 compounds) was reduced to 200 or fewer docked and 10 prioritised candidates per case, with Case C treated as an exploratory PPI stress test. LLM citation accuracy on independent PubMed verification was 88%, 78%, and 90% (pooled 85%, 23/27). No experimental assays were performed. Incurred LLM API cost was $1,450–$1,800; projected discovery-phase cost $3,450–$10,800 (lower bound). A retrospective public-target benchmark (acetylcholinesterase, PDB 4EY7) reproduced the crystallographic pose to 0.31 A but showed that the docking score alone did not enrich known actives (ROC-AUC 0.23); mechanism-based interaction filtering restored above-random early recognition (BEDROC 0.02 to 0.44), supporting the multi-evidence, human-gated design rather than docking-based ranking alone. This provides a reproducible, low-cost blueprint for computational NCE prioritisation in resource-constrained settings, not a validated drug-discovery platform; prioritised compounds are computational predictions requiring subsequent Tier 3 experimental confirmation.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI-Orchestrated Computational Drug Discovery: A Case-Study-Demonstrated Open-Source Workflow Blueprint

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Design for Additive Manufacturing tools apply predefined geometric checks, while dimensional limits require experimental validation for specific alloys, machines, and process settings. Engineers often interpret their applicability and manually coordinate assessment, redesign, and simulation. Large language models alone cannot reliably provide precise geometric measurements. This paper introduces AgenticDfAM, which coordinates reasoning agents and tools to revise designs and their assessment and construction procedures. Tools retain authority over numerical evidence. The feature-recognition and measurement tools were developed and benchmarked against reference geometries. Scripted agent replies were used to test validation of communication between agentic stages, error handling, and recovery. Invalid inter-agent messages were rejected by semantic validators. Across computational case studies, three redesign strategies remove all reference violations while exposing material and distortion tradeoffs. Thermal feedback lowers a part’s predicted layer-scale peak temperature by 160 °C. In a support design experiment, support above an intended contact surface was identified by a reviewer and corrected by the agent after diagnosis of the construction code. The correction was verified on curved and flat targets and reused in four autonomous clamp runs, with returns to support construction reduced from ten to five. The workflow investigates issues beyond prescribed checks while retaining verifiable engineering evidence.
evidence_items.title: AgenticDfAM: An agentic workﬂow automates design for additive manufacturing through traceable adaptive assessment and multicriteria redesigns

evidence_items.summary: The Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) standardizes posttreatment MRI response assessment in patients with diffuse gliomas but requires complex integration of imaging trends, medication effects, and radiation timing. An end-to-end multiagent large language model and convolutional neural network system for automated BTRADS classification was developed and evaluated. Five hundred nine consecutive posttreatment glioma MRI examinations (March 2017-July 2021) from a single center were retrospectively evaluated. An extractor agent identified clinical variables from notes using gpt-oss (OpenAI, 20-billion parameters). A scorer agent applied BTRADS decision logic integrating these with quantitative volumetrics. System accuracy was compared against initial assessments, using expert annotation as the reference standard. Four hundred ninety-two examinations were evaluable. Overall system accuracy was 76.0% (374/492) versus 57.5% (283/492) for initial assessments, an absolute difference of +18.5 percentage points ( P < .001). Cohen kappa between the system and the reference standard was 0.71. The system achieved high sensitivity in context-dependent categories (BT-1b; 100%; BT-1a, 92.7%; BT-3a, 87.5%) and moderate sensitivity for threshold-dependent categories (BT-3c, 74.8%; BT-2, 69.2%; BT-4, 69.3%; BT-3b, 57.1%). The BT-4 positive predictive value was 92.9%. These results support further evaluation of this system as a clinical decision-support tool, with local open-weight inference preserving data privacy. ©RSNA, 2026
evidence_items.title: Agentic Automation of BT-RADS Scoring Using an End-to-End System for                     Standardized Glioma Follow-up Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed. Learned unmasking policies improve the speed--accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter. We view supervised policies as distilling a decoding procedure through a teacher and examine independently what the teacher labels as committable, on which states the policy imitates it, what the policy observes, and how much the number of function evaluations (NFE) must decrease to offset policy overhead. We find that labeling predictions matching the final output is overly permissive at low NFE, and hidden states are weak alone but can complement confidence. About a 10% NFE reduction suffices to offset policy overhead for policies up to 7.5M parameters across tested settings. We therefore train a policy on trajectory-contraction targets, which accept only commitments staying on a reference trajectory, using confidence and hidden states. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the resulting 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy--NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, is competitive at moderate targets on MATH-500 and HumanEval, and largely transfers to Dream-7B-Instruct.
evidence_items.title: What Makes a Good Unmasking Policy? A Controlled Study of Learned Unmasking in Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.
evidence_items.title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires 32times fewer retrieval queries and 2048times fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.
evidence_items.title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis
